item.title: Exclusive: Thune believes Trump is open on AI guardrails despite public defiance
item.description:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune says he doesn't believe President Trump is "really dug in" against guardrails for AI, despite Trump's public campaign against restricting the technology.

Why it matters: Thune told Axios he spoke privately with Trump as the AI issue was getting "pretty hot" a few weeks ago and believes some of Trump's strong pushback is against public "paranoia and noise around the subject."

  • "I don't think it's an issue that he's really dug in on," Thune told Axios. Thune reads Trump's position as a preference for companies coming up with ways to secure their systems, rather than Congress or the administration. That approach relies more on experts to provide guidance.
  • Trump has called recent fears around AI safety a "hoax."
  • "I do think that the threats are real," Thune told Axios in an interview on Wednesday at his Capitol office.

Zoom out: Thune has Trump's skepticism in one ear and tech leader alarm in the other.

  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called Thune to discuss AI safety before sounding his latest public alarm on the risks of AI, Thune told Axios.
  • The two also talked about Thune's AI bill.

What to watch: "I think you have to have at least some sort of a plan and some guardrails around it, which is what I think our bill does," Thune said, referencing the bill he has introduced with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) in past years.

  • "But I do also think that there are people who are... doing a lot of fear mongering," Thune added.
  • Thune's bill, which has passed out of committee last Congress but has not yet been reintroduced this Congress, puts the onus on tech companies to mitigate AI risks. It also requires AI companies to report on any serious risks with frontier models and to come up with plans to address the concerns. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) has been involved with the bill this Congress.
  • Thune said Klobuchar is trying to get more Democratic co-sponsors on board — including Sens. Chris Coons (D-Del.) and Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) — before re-introducing the bill.

The details: Democrats have two main sticking points, according to Thune:

  • Pre-deployment testing is something companies can opt into in the bill language. Democrats want it mandated.
  • Cantwell is asking for AI rulemaking authority at the Department of Commerce. Thune worries rulemaking authority could give the executive too much power.

The bottom line: Thune is able to pull on experience working on AI policy. If he had not become leader, he would have again chaired the Commerce committee, which has jurisdiction over much of the issue.

Go deeper: "We have a choice": AI leaders sound alarm at UN

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a more complete version of Thune's quote on Trump's position on AI guardrails.

item.title: Dems grapple with how to pace the AI race
item.description:
The left's push to rein in AI is taking shape on two fronts: slowing advanced development at home, and weakening China's progress abroad.

Why it matters: The nation is locked in a moment of mass anxiety about runaway AI, but the range of views on how to regulate it are as varied as the what-ifs about social, economic and security impacts.

  • There's agreement among the left something has to be done, but a series of Wednesday events demonstrated there are multiple priorities — but not a clear leading voice — on AI.

Driving the news: Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders (Vt.) and fellow progressive Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) introduced legislation Wednesday to ban superintelligence and pause advanced development until a new, Cabinet-level Department of Artificial Intelligence sets guardrails.

  • "I understand that I may be called an alarmist for introducing this bill," Sanders said in a Wednesday call with reporters, "but I'd rather be called an alarmist than a father and grandfather who is asleep at the wheel."
  • Casar emphasized that "we cannot wait for an international agreement to pause dangerous development in the United States. China trains their models off of American models, so stopping dangerous AI development in America will slow down dangerous advancements in China."

Zoom out: Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) took up another regulatory approach Wednesday, focused on restricting foreign AI capabilities.

  • "President Trump must draw a hard line. Do not weaken America's export controls. Do not give China greater access to the advanced chips and chip-making equipment it needs to close the gap," Schumer said in a plea to move forward on related bipartisan legislation.
  • Schumer argued that calls to pause AI research and the focus on winning the AI race "are not at all contradictory."

Casar said the goal of his and Sanders' legislation is to "stop the race towards disaster."

  • Sanders has been forceful in calls for immediate congressional action, saying Wednesday that "we cannot simply sit by idly and wait for advanced AI to cause the next 9/11 or Chernobyl."

Between the lines: Even within the progressive camp, there's not complete cohesion on the specifics of confronting the AI buildout, Axios' Maria Curi writes.

  • Warren has backed a pause on advanced artificial intelligence, but she's stopped short of endorsing a ban on superintelligence, like Sanders.

Possible 2028 contenders diverge as well, with several stopping short of echoing Sanders' call to pause development. Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel previously told Axios that "a pause is fine — but then what?"

  • Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), another member of the party's progressive wing who has called to ban self-improving AI, is also set to convene a virtual hearing Wednesday calling for a U.S.-China agreement to pace AI development — yet another potential regulatory approach.

State of play: The three proposals come as Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping, with AI a likely focus of the talks as the rival nations discuss ways to manage shared risks, per Axios' Courtenay Brown.

  • Trump has insisted the U.S. must keep an edge over China, warning that "whoever wins" the AI race "wins."

The bottom line: Which idea (or ideas) Democrats in Congress champion could become a key issue for the November midterms.

Go deeper: AI boom can withstand a development slowdown

item.title: Cook nudges three Senate races toward Democrats
item.description:
Senate races in Georgia, Kansas and South Carolina were reclassified with a nudge toward Democrats in the latest analysis from the closely watched Cook Political Report.

The big picture: To win the Senate, Democrats must net four seats in November.

  • Tighter races in Republican strongholds like Kansas and South Carolina could force the GOP to devote resources beyond the core battlegrounds.

The latest: In the latest Cook ratings, Kansas moved from "Likely Republican" to "Lean Republican." South Carolina shifted from "Solid Republican" to "Likely Republican."

  • Georgia and the seat held by Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) changed from "Lean Democrat" to "Likely Democrat."

By the numbers: There are six Republican-held Senate seats rated by Cook as a "Toss Up" or better for Democrats.

  • The Georgia shift makes a Republican pickup there less likely, while the Kansas move expands the map of competitive seats for Democrats.

Zoom out: The midterms environment is improving for Democrats amid voter discontent about gas prices, the cost of living and the broader handling of the Iran war.

Flashback: Last month, Cook shifted Senate and gubernatorial races in Texas and Iowa in Democrats' favor.

item.title: Chicago mayor proposes 12-month moratorium on new data centers
item.description:
Chicago could halt new data center development within city limits for a year.

Why it matters: Data centers' growing demand for electricity and water could affect residents' utility bills and the environment, and city leaders want more time to study those impacts.

The latest: Mayor Brandon Johnson, along with a group of alders, is pushing for a 12-month moratorium while the city develops a "comprehensive regulatory framework" for data centers.

  • There are 39 active data centers in Chicago, according to the city.

Details: The proposal would give Johnson's Data Centers Task Force time to study the industry's impacts on clean air, clean water and energy use.

What they're saying: "Chicago is open for business, but we are not for sale," Johnson said in a statement. "We welcome innovation, investment, and the jobs and opportunities that come with it, but growth must be done responsibly and in a way that protects the health, safety and quality of life of Chicago residents."

Context: The announcement comes as other alders, including Ald. Bill Conway (34th), push their own ordinance to regulate data centers.

  • "The Mayor's proposal risks months if not years of debate and litigation, all while data centers keep building, polluting, and spiking utility bills with zero community input," Conway said in a statement.
  • Conway's ordinance would immediately subject data centers to additional zoning requirements and community and environmental reviews.

Zoom out: Chicago wouldn't be alone. At least a half-dozen major U.S. cities, including Seattle, Charlotte, Baltimore, Cincinnati, Cleveland and Oklahoma City, have temporarily halted or restricted new data center development while considering new regulations.

  • At the state level, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has paused new tax incentives for data centers, but has said he doesn't have the authority to impose a statewide moratorium on construction.
  • Illinois cities like Bloomington, Carbondale, Effingham, West Chicago and Mattoon have already paused new data center development or expansion.

The other side: "As the City of Chicago faces significant and continuing fiscal and budgetary challenges, it's important to recognize that data centers are net revenue generators that provide billions of dollars in economic investment," Data Center Coalition's Brad Tietz said in a statement.

  • "Unfortunately, the Mayor's proposed moratorium sends another signal that Chicago is closed for business."

Friction point: Communities across the country are pushing back against proposed data centers over concerns about electricity demand, water use, pollution and other impacts.

  • President Trump has criticized efforts to restrict them, writing on social media: "The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor. If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign."

What's next: Both proposals will now make their way through the City Council, setting up a debate over how the city should regulate new data center development.

item.title: Iran president: We have been "victims of terrorism"
item.description:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian forcefully rejected President Trump's portrayal of Iran as a source of terrorism at the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, insisting instead that Iranians are "victims of terrorism."

Why it matters: Pezeshkian used one of the world's biggest diplomatic stages to directly challenge Trump on U.S. soil — as the U.S.-Israel war with Iran rages on.

What he's saying: "The United States president described us as terrorists," Pezeshkian said in a roughly 18-minute speech.

  • "We have been the victims of terrorism… Those who are terrorists and train and protect terrorists describe us as such. We have only defended ourselves. We are not terrorists."
  • "Our innocent people have been the targets of cowardly attacks and aggressions imposed upon our country, and we defended ourselves with utmost strength," he said.
  • "We live in a world in which the powerful, instead of thinking about humanity, justice, fairness, and democracy, they seem to be the protectors and creators of instability and destruction."

Zoom in: Pezeshkian cited attacks that he blamed on the U.S., including strikes that killed children.

  • He pointed to the deaths of more than 150 Iranians at an elementary school in Minab, including more than 120 children.
  • A recent UN report found "reasonable grounds to believe" the U.S. committed a war crime in the strike.
  • While the U.S. has not released findings of an investigation related to the attack, the AP has found evidence that at least one U.S. missile struck the school.
  • Pezeshkian also mentioned the alleged deaths of children playing at a sports hall and an adjacent school after they were struck by a U.S.-made ballistic missile.

Between the lines: The same UN report found that Iran's crackdown on protesters likely constituted "crimes against humanity."

  • The report cited tactics including "murder, imprisonment, torture and other inhumane acts" as "part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians."

What to watch: U.S. and Iranian officials held three hours of indirect talks on the sidelines of the UN on Tuesday, with Trump calling the meeting "very productive" and suggestions a deal remains possible.

  • Iran has downplayed the breakthrough, saying its negotiating position has not changed — underscoring how far apart the two sides remain even as diplomacy continues.

Go deeper: UN report: U.S. may have committed war crimes in Iran

item.title: Scoop: Trump's Board of Peace to unveil $2.45 billion Gaza recovery plan
item.description:
President Trump's Board of Peace will unveil a six-month, $2.45 billion recovery plan for Gaza at a meeting of its members on Wednesday.

Why it matters: The 66-project proposal offers one of the most comprehensive roadmaps yet for what the early months of post-war reconstruction and governance in Gaza would look like.

  • The plan is a result of a year of work by dozens of people both on the Board of Peace, which includes 28 member countries, and in the Palestinian technocratic government.
  • It includes projected spending for temporary housing, rubble removal, hospital repairs, economic recovery and the deployment of a multinational security force, according to a copy of the plan obtained by Axios.
  • "The plan shows how to stand up a government from nothing, an economy from shambles and a territory from disaster," a Board of Peace official said.

Yes, but: For the plan to move forward, the Board of Peace needs Israel and Hamas to cooperate.

  • While the Netanyahu government has agreed in principle to aspects of the plan that have been previously discussed, it refused to start implementing it, mainly for domestic political reasons ahead of the elections.
  • And while Hamas agreed in principle to disarm, it hasn't been tested yet, partly because Israel won't implement a 14-day ceasefire before the demilitarization process starts.
  • The Board of Peace hopes that after the Israeli elections on Oct. 27 and the formation of a new Israeli government, the Gaza recovery process can finally start.
  • But the election is unlikely to yield a clear winner, resulting in a caretaker government and a political stalemate. That could further undermine implementation of the Gaza proposal.

The big picture: The plan estimates physical damage in Gaza at $35.2 billion and says full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4 billion over the next decade.

Zoom in: The plan divides the 66 projects into six areas: infrastructure development, human development, economic acceleration, digital transformation, legal affairs, and peace and security:

Infrastructure accounts for the largest share, at roughly $1 billion, including about $400 million for temporary shelters, $275 million for rubble and unexploded ordnance clearance, $50 million for hospital rehabilitation and $30 million to repair Gaza's badly damaged road network.

  • The plan also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar-power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects.

Security-related projects account for roughly $885 million, making them another major component of the proposal.

  • The plan allocates about $275 million for a permanent hardened site in Rafah capable of supporting 5,000 personnel from the International Stabilization Force (ISF) and another $140 million to recruit, train, equip and deploy a multinational security contingent.
  • Another $120 million would go toward mobilizing Palestinian police. While thousands of Palestinians from Gaza have been selected and vetted to serve in the new Gaza police force, Israel has blocked them from leaving Gaza for training in Egypt.
  • $20 million would fund a weapons buy-back program offering incentives for weapons and ammunition to be surrendered by Hamas and members of other armed groups and safely disposed of.
  • According to the plan, the Palestinian technocratic government would also eventually take over management of Gaza's border crossings with Israel and Egypt for both goods and passengers.

What to watch: One of the most immediate priorities is moving Palestinians out of tents.

  • Roughly $400 million is earmarked for insulated caravans for displaced Palestinians currently living in tents.
  • Separately, the UAE would fund a pilot "Emirati Neighborhood" in the Rafah area designed to house 50,000 people currently living in tents, with independent utilities.
  • The plan also allocates roughly $300 million for health, education and welfare programs.

Between the lines: The proposal isn't limited to emergency relief. It is also intended to establish the infrastructure of a functioning Palestinian administration and restart Gaza's private sector.

  • Projects include a digital ID system, digital payments, 4G connectivity, electronic health and education systems, grants to restart small businesses and a new Gaza investment fund.
  • The Board of Peace and the Palestinian technocratic government say recovery should be Palestinian-led and based on "Palestinian ownership."

What's next: A key challenge is funding. At the moment, the Board of Peace and the Palestinian technocratic government haven't secured the entire $2.45 billion.

  • But Board of Peace officials say they don't need the entire sum immediately when the new Palestinian technocratic government enters Gaza.
  • The officials expressed confidence that once the political hurdles are cleared, donor countries will step up to fund the various projects.

The latest: Representatives from 35 countries attended the Board of Peace briefing, including from the EU, UN and several countries connected to the Board of Peace, even though those countries are not actual members of the Board.

  • Trump's senior adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner, who spearheaded the administration's Gaza effort, joined with White House envoy Steve Witkoff, Board of Peace High Representative Nickolay Mladenov and the head of the Palestinian technocratic government, Ali Shaath, in calling on donor countries to support the Gaza plan.
  • "We want to build something new in Gaza, better one, that gives peace a lasting chance," Mladenov said at the event.
  • He added that the Board of Peace discussion with Israel "is not easy" because of the election. "Everything now is more sensitive," he said. "We wish things would have taken less time, but we make slow and steady progress."
  • "There are no shortcuts. No Plan B. We will all work to have this plan succeed," Witkoff said.

item.title: Trump pursues last-ditch hunt for voter fraud
item.description:
The Trump administration says Americans should prepare between now and Election Day for a wave of new arrests and prosecutions over alleged non-citizen voter fraud. Why it matters: The Trump administration is deploying hundreds of federal investigators and attorneys to pursue President Trump's long-running fixation — and test a broader Republican claim that tougher enforcement will uncover far more illegal voting.

  • "This initiative is a tier one priority," a Justice Department official told reporters on Tuesday. "It's a top priority for the attorney general and for the White House."

The big picture: Across the country, there are now 1,600 open cases of potential voter fraud and 160 people have been arrested, a Homeland Security Investigations official said Tuesday.

  • HSI agents have been requesting and combing through publicly available voter data to find cases of non-citizens registering to vote or voting when they're ineligible. The FBI has been working on these cases too.
  • DOJ has charged 24 immigrants this calendar year following the prioritization, according to agency press releases. The accused are a mixture of undocumented immigrations and legal residents.
  • The number of prosecutions will "rise significantly each week going forward from now until the election," the DOJ official said.

Zoom in: To support these investigations, which the HSI official called agent-time intensive, Homeland Security staff have shifted work time from other priorities.

  • HSI agents typically investigate smuggling, trafficking, financial fraud and sexual exploitation crimes.

The intrigue: Staff usually focused on finding immigration fraud at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, the office for legal immigration, have also been tasked with searching for possible non-citizens registered in state voter files.

  • This staff sent referrals to HSI to investigate, according to the New York Times, and flagged the potential non-citizens by the thousands to state election officials.
  • For three weeks, the fraud team was tasked with reviewing voter files and not allowed to do other work, a person familiar with the agency's work told Axios.

The other side: Instances of mistaken registrations and cases of non-citizen voting are rare, but they've long been investigated by the federal government.

  • The extent of this administration's efforts to prioritize searching for these cases is novel for the federal government and the local election officials involved.
  • "It's not typical and it's not appropriate," a former senior Justice Department official told Axios in July.

Between the lines: New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherril revealed in July that 6,600 non-citizens were registered to vote through a software error.

  • The DOJ official said there are also similar system errors registering people who aren't intending to register in other states.
  • But they declined to say whether any government officials or vendors responsible for these errors would be held responsible as individual voters now are.

The bottom line: "These investigations and these indictments are a major deterrent for this election" against illegal voting, Mike Davis, founder of the Article III Project, a legal affairs-focused nonprofit closely aligned with the president.

  • "There's a new sheriff in town: His name is Donald Trump, and if illegals vote in our elections, they will be prosecuted and deported."

item.title: The All-In-ification of Trump's AI agenda
item.description:
President Trump's accelerationist AI doctrine increasingly bears the stamp of the "All-In" podcast, whose tech-investor network now feeds ideas and talent directly into the White House.

Why it matters: An unlikely marriage of convenience between MAGA and Silicon Valley has proved remarkably durable, deepening as Trump sheds support elsewhere and stakes more of his legacy on dominating the AI race.

Zoom in: No figure has done more to bridge the two worlds than David Sacks, the "All-In" co-host who spent Trump's first year as his AI czar and remains a powerful outside adviser with direct access to the president.

  • Sacks helped build Trump's original AI agenda around a simple premise: move fast, sweep away regulatory barriers and treat China — not catastrophic risk — as the overriding threat.
  • Anthropic's highly capable Mythos model posed the first serious challenge to that doctrine in May, rattling the White House enough to consider pre-release oversight of frontier models.
  • But Trump watered down the 90-day review plan after Sacks and industry leaders warned that three months amounted to an eternity in frontier AI — and could slow U.S. labs as China raced ahead.

Zoom out: Sacks left the White House but not Trump's inner circle, shaping AI policy as co-chair of the president's science council while the broader "All-In" network embeds itself deeper across Trumpworld.

  • David Friedberg serves on the same council alongside investor Marc Andreessen, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg and other tech leaders — putting half of "All-In"'s core cast on the president's formal science-policy panel.
  • Chamath Palihapitiya, another co-host and prominent Trump booster, is among the names being floated for the new AI czar job Trump announced last weekend.
  • Brad Gerstner, a frequent fill-in on the podcast, helped conceive Trump Accounts and became one of the program's chief evangelists.

The intrigue: Jason Calacanis, the show's moderator, is the political outlier — frequently criticizing Trump on Iran and inflation while otherwise aligning with his co-hosts on the revolutionary nature of AI.

Between the lines: Few platforms better capture the zeitgeist of AI accelerationism than "All-In," where the movement's leading investors, executives and political allies increasingly converge.

  • After former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon's safety warnings exploded across Washington, the hosts devoted much of their next episode to portraying the backlash as an orchestrated "doomer" campaign.
  • Three days later, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang paused his live "All-In" Summit interview to take a call from Trump, who drew a raucous reception as he dismissed AI catastrophe fears as a "hoax."

What they're saying: White House spokesperson Kush Desai said Trump "has always listened to a variety of opinions from a variety of subject matter experts" and argued that his open line to tech leaders has helped widen America's technological lead.

  • "The fact that this President maintains an open line of communication with tech leaders instead of castigating them, as the Biden administration had done, is a major reason why America's technological and innovative lead has widened since President Trump came into office," Desai said.

What to watch: "All-In" and the accelerationist wing of Silicon Valley are tying themselves unusually tightly to one president and one governing philosophy.

  • Sacks, for example, has blessed a $100 million-plus midterm operation built to advance Trump's AI agenda and punish candidates who favor tougher regulation.
  • Inside AI labs, that political fusion is feeding a deeper fear: that warnings about catastrophic risk will become coded as anti-Trump politics, turning AI safety into yet another partisan litmus test.

item.title: Uber's robotaxi edge: human drivers
item.description:
Uber is betting billions on a driverless future, but the secret to making the economics work could be — surprise! — its vast army of human drivers.

Why it matters: Uber believes a hybrid network of robots and people can keep its expensive autonomous vehicles busier, and therefore more profitable, than fleets made up entirely of robotaxis.

The big picture: Think of a high-tech robotaxi like an airplane: It costs money whether it's carrying passengers or sitting on the ground.

  • The more trips each vehicle makes, the more revenue Uber and its robotaxi partners can squeeze from that expensive asset, offsetting the fixed costs of the technology, vehicle financing, insurance, depot space and other infrastructure.

Between the lines: Ride-hailing is a supply-driven business, and robotaxis aren't a substitute for drivers, Uber says — they're an additional form of supply.

  • With greater supply comes lower prices and shorter wait times, which means increased reliability.
  • That stimulates more demand, and ultimately makes the ride-hailing pie bigger.
  • That's Uber's theory.

Robotaxi economics remain unproven, Uber's own head of autonomous mobility and delivery, Sarfraz Maredia, tells Axios.

  • It's still early, and no company is making money yet operating them, nor is anyone yet operating them at massive scale.
  • Whether AVs and all that's needed to support a fleet — including charging infrastructure and maintenance — will ultimately be cheaper than today's ride-hailing model "very much has yet to be proven," Maredia says. "The unit economics today have a long way to go."

Uber's bet is that its mix of human drivers and AVs will produce better returns.

How it works: In a hybrid network — and Lyft has a similar philosophy —AVs would handle the steady "base load" of everyday demand.

  • Human drivers, meanwhile, would provide extra capacity during rush hour, bad weather, concerts and other demand spikes.
  • Maredia points to late nights as an example: Uber can recharge robotaxis when electricity is cheapest while human drivers handle the bar-closing rush.

So far, Uber says, robotaxis are taking shorter city-center trips, while drivers get longer, more lucrative ones.

  • "You could argue that the AVs are getting the scraps," CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told Fast Company earlier this year.

That flexibility is an advantage, Uber says.

  • A robotaxi operator needs enough cars to handle its busiest periods — leaving expensive AVs sitting idle when demand falls.
  • Uber, by contrast, can size its robotaxi fleet for normal demand and summon more human drivers when needed.
  • Drivers only get paid when they're working, whereas robotaxis cost money even when they're idle.

Reality check: Drivers will be displaced eventually, and Uber doesn't argue that point.

  • Part-time drivers who use Uber as a safety net — women, caregivers and lower-income workers — will be disproportionally affected, the company acknowledges.
  • Others will have to work longer or at different times and places to earn the same amount, the company says.
  • But a hybrid network will help ease that transition, it says.

By the numbers: Uber says trips are up in Austin and Atlanta, where Waymo AVs are sharing the Uber app with drivers, and driver earnings have stayed consistent.

  • Uber says Waymos on its network in Austin and Atlanta are completing about 30% more trips per vehicle per day than AVs in other major robotaxi markets.

Yes, but: Independent research from Gridwise, an app that lets gig drivers track earnings, expenses and mileage, had different findings.

  • It compared earnings for Uber and Lyft drivers in the second quarter with the same period two years ago and found base pay per hour was lower in San Francisco and Los Angeles, where they are competing with Waymo.
  • In Austin, where Waymos are exclusively available on Uber, base pay and gross pay per hour rose less than rideshare drivers in other parts of the country, Gridwise found, suggesting AV growth could already be putting pressure on driver earnings.

The bottom line: Humans may make Uber's robotaxi math work. Whether the math works as well for the humans is less certain.

item.title: Poll: Americans see rule of law declining in U.S.
item.description:
Data: Charles F. Kettering Foundation and Gallup; Note: Values shown may not total 100% due to rounding and exclusion of "don't know" responses; Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios Visuals

A majority of Americans say the rule of law in the U.S. is weaker now than a decade ago, when Donald Trump was first elected president, according to a massive new survey of more than 23,000 U.S. adults.

Driving the news: 78% of those responding to the survey by Gallup and the Charles F. Kettering Foundation for its Democracy for All Project say government officials must always follow laws and the Constitution.

  • But just 28% trust that political leaders will be held accountable if they don't.

Zoom in: Throwing out incumbents was respondents' top choice (17%) when asked what one step could be taken to most improve U.S. democracy. That response reflects a prominent theme of a midterm campaign that's shadowed by widespread voter dissatisfaction.

  • Other steps suggested by survey respondents included electoral reform and improved voting access (13%) and limiting executive power (9%).

One stunning stat: Older Republicans (65+) appear significantly less trusting of election officials now than just a year ago, with 42% saying it's reasonable to assume that election officials acted improperly if election outcomes are surprising, up from 30%.

By the numbers: The share of Americans who say the rule of law is weaker now than in 2016 is four times higher than the share who think it's stronger (56% compared with 14%), while 29% say it's unchanged. Democrats and independents were much likelier than Republicans to say it's weaker.

  • The top reason respondents cited for getting involved in a social or political cause: Feeling an important right or freedom is being threatened (27%), followed by feeling you can make a difference (26%) and seeing officials abuse or misuse power (19%).
  • 57% said they prefer candidates who challenge powerful or established interests, while 42% prefer candidates who work within the establishment.

What we're watching: Two-thirds of Americans said democracy is the best form of government, the same as last year. But across several measures, the data show the public more pessimistic now than in 2025:

  • 49% say they don't agree with the idea that U.S. leaders are committed to having a strong democracy, up from 44% a year ago.
  • 47% say they're comfortable openly expressing opinions about government and laws, down from 52%.
  • 56% say democracy is doing poorly, up from 51% the year before. That sense is largely being driven by rising concerns from Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, while Democrats and neutral independents already were highly critical.
  • Respondents give the state of democracy higher marks at the local level than the national level.

What they're saying: "People care about democracy, and that is something worth building on," said Derek Barker, senior program officer for research initiatives at Kettering.

  • "Right now, it's a matter of getting through this period where people are really concerned about how it's performing and how leaders are acting in office."

Methodology: The Gallup Poll conducted this survey for the Gallup-Kettering Foundation's Democracy for All Project. The survey was completed by 23,683 U.S. adults, aged 18 and older, including 10,800 respondents recruited for the study and 12,883 supplemental respondents from a third-party sample provider.

  • 21,652 respondents completed the survey as a web survey April 24-May 21, 2026, and 2,031 respondents completed the survey as a mail survey April 24-June 10, 2026.
  • For results based on this sample, the maximum margin of sampling error, which takes into account the design effect from weighting, is ±1 percentage point at the 95% confidence level.

A majority of Americans say the rule of law in the U.S. is weaker now than a decade ago, when Donald Trump was first elected president, according to a massive new survey of more than 23,000 U.S. adults.

Driving the news: 78% of those responding to the survey by Gallup and the Charles F. Kettering Foundation for its Democracy for All Project say government officials must always follow laws and the Constitution.

  • But just 28% trust that political leaders will be held accountable if they don't.

Zoom in: Throwing out incumbents was respondents' top choice (17%) when asked what one step could be taken to most improve U.S. democracy. That response reflects a prominent theme of a midterm campaign that's shadowed by widespread voter dissatisfaction.

  • Other steps suggested by survey respondents included electoral reform and improved voting access (13%) and limiting executive power (9%).

One stunning stat: Older Republicans (65+) appear significantly less trusting of election officials now than just a year ago, with 42% saying it's reasonable to assume that election officials acted improperly if election outcomes are surprising, up from 30%.

By the numbers: The share of Americans who say the rule of law is weaker now than in 2016 is four times higher than the share who think it's stronger (56% compared with 14%), while 29% say it's unchanged. Democrats and independents were much likelier than Republicans to say it's weaker.

  • The top reason respondents cited for getting involved in a social or political cause: Feeling an important right or freedom is being threatened (27%), followed by feeling you can make a difference (26%) and seeing officials abuse or misuse power (19%).
  • 57% said they prefer candidates who challenge powerful or established interests, while 42% prefer candidates who work within the establishment.

What we're watching: Two-thirds of Americans said democracy is the best form of government, the same as last year. But across several measures, the data show the public more pessimistic now than in 2025:

  • 49% say they don't agree with the idea that U.S. leaders are committed to having a strong democracy, up from 44% a year ago.
  • 47% say they're comfortable openly expressing opinions about government and laws, down from 52%.
  • 56% say democracy is doing poorly, up from 51% the year before. That sense is largely being driven by rising concerns from Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, while Democrats and neutral independents already were highly critical.
  • Respondents give the state of democracy higher marks at the local level than the national level.

What they're saying: "People care about democracy, and that is something worth building on," said Derek Barker, senior program officer for research initiatives at Kettering.

  • "Right now, it's a matter of getting through this period where people are really concerned about how it's performing and how leaders are acting in office."

Methodology: The Gallup Poll conducted this survey for the Gallup-Kettering Foundation's Democracy for All Project. The survey was completed by 23,683 U.S. adults, aged 18 and older, including 10,800 respondents recruited for the study and 12,883 supplemental respondents from a third-party sample provider.

  • 21,652 respondents completed the survey as a web survey April 24-May 21, 2026, and 2,031 respondents completed the survey as a mail survey April 24-June 10, 2026.
  • For results based on this sample, the maximum margin of sampling error, which takes into account the design effect from weighting, is ±1 percentage point at the 95% confidence level.

item.title: AI labs are cutting model costs - and it could help them slow down safely
item.description:
The shift of the AI frontier toward more powerful, lower-cost models could pave the way for safely slowing development, experts say.

Why it matters: Top U.S. startups including OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as other AI players, have to develop a financially viable path to allow them to slow development. Otherwise financial incentives will be too powerful.

Driving the news: The health of the entire U.S. economy now rests in part on the AI boom. Yet the companies at the center of the race are burning far more cash than they take in, and will be for the foreseeable future.

  • Their top executives have also shown unusual solidarity in expressing a desire to slow the pace of model development due to a troubling series of incidents in which rogue AI agents hacked outside companies.

Between the lines: To enable a slowdown, in a financial sense, the companies have to find a way to build a value proposition to users that isn't solely rooted in the most mind-blowing intelligence imaginable. That's because remaining at the so-called frontier of capabilities requires a treadmill of never-ending — and mind-boggling spending — to keep up.

  • Slowing the extent of that spending, some of which is used for the computing firepower needed to train new models, would help the companies generate better returns.
  • That wouldn't necessarily threaten spending on computing, data centers and infrastructure such as upgrading the electric grid, according to some economists and AI pros. Those investments will still be needed in order to service demand for AI usage that continues to skyrocket.

Catch up quick: Everybody gets a new model this week, and the one thing they all have in common is that they're cheaper than ever without forgoing top intelligence.

  • OpenAI, Anthropic and SpaceX all emphasized the relatively low costs of their new models this week, as well as their ability to outperform some of their own top systems from only a few months ago.
  • Chinese models including DeepSeek have done the same. DeepSeek's V4.1 Flash, released earlier this month, is now number one on OpenRouter's leaderboard with a 172% spike in usage this week.

Reality check: The rationale for the price cuts also goes beyond safety.

  • In a report sent to clients, Citadel Securities found that falling per-token costs are fueling enough additional usage to increase overall AI spending, meaning higher profits for labs even as they cut costs.
  • This paradox is why the AI labs have a rich history of effectively cutting prices for models over time: it increases their customer base and their profits.

The bottom line: The race to win on AI costs could be the very thing that allows the labs to enable the slowdown they are seeking.

item.title: FBI investigating claims that a major cybercrime group stole sensitive personnel data
item.description:
A notorious cybercrime group is claiming they stole more than 2 terabytes of data that includes detailed personal information about thousands of FBI employees and job applicants.

Why it matters: Cybercriminals and state-sponsored attackers have penetrated U.S. IT systems for years, but stealing detailed and sensitive information about FBI employees is brazen, cyber experts told Axios.

  • Cybercriminals are known to trade leaked information on the dark web, a prospect that would leave the data up for grabs from the highest bidder.

Driving the news: ShinyHunters, a group that's broken into numerous institutions, said in a post on its dark-web site Tuesday that it stole "very sensitive data on almost ALL FBI agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job."

An FBI spokesperson said in a statement the bureau is "aware of claims regarding unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov and is currently investigating."

What to watch: Cynthia Kaiser, a former top official in the FBI's cyber division, told Axios that when a hacker targets the FBI, expect the bureau "to marshal additional resources to bring them more quickly to justice."

The big picture: While the breach is likely to bring more law enforcement attention to ShinyHunters in the short term, the long tail impact is greater on the FBI employees and their families whose information was stolen, Allan Liska, a threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future, told Axios.

  • "The data is out there and has likely been repeatedly downloaded and passed around to other threat actors," Liska said.

Axios has not been able to corroborate that the data stolen is legitimate or recent, but cybersecurity researchers confirmed that the attack appears legitimate. 404 Media obtained a sample of the stolen data, which appears to include information about 5,000 alleged agents.

Zoom in: ShinyHunters told Axios in an email that the stolen data includes names, FBI agent statuses, emails, phone numbers, home addresses and "sometimes even spouse information," including their Social Security numbers.

  • The group also claims it broke into the FBI's criminal justice, HR and other services.
  • ShinyHunters also said it seized and defaced the FBI's jobs webpage via a zero-day in Oracle's PeopleSoft platform. The site was still offline as of Tuesday afternoon.
Screenshot: FBI career page on Sept. 22.

Catch up quick: ShinyHunters says its hack is not financially motivated. Instead, the group is pushing the FBI to retract statements it made about how ShinyHunters operates.

  • In a May advisory, the FBI warned the hackers "commonly use harassment strategies, sending threatening text messages and phone calls to victims and their family members, and in some cases, swatting."
  • ShinyHunters claims this isn't true and told Axios that it believes these claims have been tied to their group because "other low-skilled threat actors" have been using the group's name in their attacks.

Threat level: Andrew Brandt, principal threat intelligence incident commander at Huntress, told Axios that a major concern is over whether ShinyHunters chooses to sell the data to other criminal or nation-state hackers.

  • "It doesn't take much imagination to picture scenarios where employees or their families could be threatened or harmed by this kind of information being released," Brandt said.

item.title: GOP breaking with an unpopular Trump
item.description:
Congressional Republicans are increasingly breaking with an unpopular president on foreign policy and pocketbook issues as they try to stop their majorities from slipping away.

Why it matters: They aren't engaged in a full-scale revolt against President Trump, but some Republicans are testing new ways to distance themselves from him — a sign of their election anxiety.

Driving the news: Trump — facing a barrage of demands from Republican lawmakers to impose a ban on diesel exports — pulled a rare about-face Tuesday, saying on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York that he'll support a ban.

  • Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), along with Iowa GOP Reps. Ashley Hinson and Mariannette Miller-Meeks, were among those calling for a ban to ease skyrocketing diesel costs for U.S. farmers and truckers.
  • Sullivan and Hinson are in tight Senate races.

Just on Tuesday: Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) railed on the Senate floor at Trump's decision to host Chinese President Xi Jinping this week for a state dinner.

  • Wicker urged Trump to "keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly" at the U.S.
  • Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) called for the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. over his foreign business dealings and the hundreds of thousands of dollars he allegedly received from a Russian oligarch for his wedding.
  • "If your family's involved in the [presidency], then you ought to be very transparent," Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), a close Trump ally, told Axios last week when asked about the reporting on Trump Jr.'s wedding.

On Iran: The Senate is expected to vote this week on a war powers resolution. Leadership can't guarantee it won't get the Republican votes needed to pass.

  • "We're constantly, of course, checking," Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said. "But I would hope that you know the team could hang together on this."
  • The House passed a war powers resolution last week in a rebuke to Trump's military campaign against Tehran — with the most Republican support yet.
  • Both Hinson and Michigan's Republican Senate candidate, former Rep. Mike Rogers, have called for the war to end.

On the trail: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) told Trump his immigration crackdown has gone too far in a new campaign ad shot in front of the White House.

  • "I think she's saying what a lot of my constituents are thinking," Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost his primary in May amid opposition from Trump, told Axios.
  • In Iowa, Hinson recently skipped a rally put on by Vice President Vance.
  • And Florida's GOP gubernatorial candidate, Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.), deleted at least eight mentions of Trump from his campaign website, the Miami Herald reported.

The bottom line: Trump's approval ratings have hit record lows at the worst possible time for Republicans — and that's reflected in lawmakers' willingness to publicly challenge him.

  • "Members are generally reflecting their base. If they really feel that way, they should say so," retiring Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) told reporters Tuesday of the GOP opposition to the Iran war.
  • "And the administration should let these people be whoever they are to win the race."

item.title: U.S. and Iran officials meet in New York to discuss ending the war
item.description:
President Trump said U.S. officials met for three hours with the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Tuesday.

  • Trump envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner attended the meeting from the U.S. side, and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi from the Iran side.
  • "Steve and Jared had a very productive meeting today with mediators of Iran," Trump said later, before meeting with Arab leaders. "I think there's a lot of momentum for them to make a deal. That's what we are hearing from everybody."
  • Iran state television said the meeting was requested by the U.S. and "driven by the need to convey Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz," which include lifting the naval blockade, releasing frozen Iranian assets and ending the war on all fronts.

Why it matters: The General Assembly offers a rare opportunity to try to break the stalemate in the war, which is approaching the seven-month mark with no signs of a breakthrough.

  • It's the first meeting between U.S. and Iranian officials since mid-June.

State of play: Trump met with representatives of nine Arab countries on Tuesday to discuss the war.

  • At the meeting, King Abdullah of Jordan called for "the utmost restraint in response to current regional escalations."
  • He said Jordan will continue to coordinate closely with the U.S. to pursue peace and stability in the region.
  • On Tuesday night, Witkoff posted on X: "Today, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, we engaged in lengthy talks with the Iranian delegation through the mediators, who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day. They successfully completed a round of discussions that we hope will prove constructive and promising. The mediators will continue their work."

What he said: In his speech before the UN General Assembly, Trump reiterated what he told Axios last week: that he has "a big decision to make" whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilating the Islamic Republic."

  • Trump said he thinks the U.S. will reach a deal with Iran after the midterms
  • "We will get it done one way or another. We will get it done and get it done fast," Trump said.
  • "It doesn't make sense for Iran not to (make a deal)," he added. "They are waiting to see how I do in the midterm elections. What they don't realize is that I am not running … I will be here for two-and-a-half years. I gave no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn't even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon."

Zoom out: Trump also made a broader case for the war, saying many presidents before him ignored the Iran threat for many years.

  • "After giving Iran every chance for a deal I took action to ensure that neither the U.S. nor any other nation will have to face such a catastrophic problem," Trump said.

Zoom in: Trump said Iran violated the ceasefire by attacking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Still, he added, the U.S. manages to get dozens of oil tankers out of the strait every night.

  • "We must be united in putting pressure on Iran. I call on all countries to join us in our pressure campaign against Iran," he said.

This story has been updated with new details.

item.title: A GOP senator wants Trump Jr. subpoenaed after Russian oligarch-funded wedding
item.description:
Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) is urging Senate Judiciary leaders to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden to investigate whether presidential family ties have been used for private family gain.

Why it matters: The Republican Curtis is pressing a Republican-led Senate committee to scrutinize President Trump's eldest son, arguing the same congressional oversight applied to Hunter Biden should apply to presidential families of both parties.

Driving the news: The Monday letter to Senate Judiciary chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and ranking member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) asks for an investigation into "private financial benefit, preferential treatment, or access" tied to presidential family relationships.

  • Curtis wants the committee to subpoena both sons to testify about "any instances in which their relationship to the President was invoked or understood to provide value."

"The latest: Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost his GOP primary earlier this year after Trump endorsed his opponent, said Tuesday he would support Curtis' request." After "Driving the news.

Catch up quick: ProPublica reported that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward Trump Jr.'s three-day wedding celebration in the Bahamas, including buying a private-island rental.

  • Curtis also cited Trump Jr.'s ties to prediction markets. Trump Jr. is a paid strategic adviser to Kalshi and sits on Polymarket's advisory board. 1789 Capital, where Trump Jr. is a partner, has invested in Polymarket.
  • Curtis also pointed to Trump family-backed cryptocurrency ventures, international real estate deals involving meetings with foreign heads of state, and Trump Jr.'s reported defense-sector investments.

What he's saying: "A toaster is a wedding gift," Curtis wrote on X. "A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden's foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now. 'Trust us' was not enough then, and it is not enough now."

For the record: The White House, Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden have not yet responded to requests for comment.

  • Hunter Biden has denied involving his father in business dealings.
  • Trump Jr. confirmed Kremlev hosted celebrations, describing it as a wedding gift from a friend. President Trump later defended the arrangement as "totally allowed" and said he had been told his son would repay Kremlev.

Flashback: House Republicans subpoenaed Hunter Biden in 2023 as part of their impeachment inquiry into then-President Biden.

  • The younger Biden testified that he did not involve his father in his business dealings.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from Sen. John Cornyn.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) is urging Senate Judiciary leaders to subpoena Donald Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden to investigate whether presidential family ties have been used for private family gain.

Why it matters: The Republican Curtis is pressing a Republican-led Senate committee to scrutinize President Trump's eldest son, arguing the same congressional oversight applied to Hunter Biden should apply to presidential families of both parties.

Driving the news: The Monday letter to Senate Judiciary chair Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and ranking member Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) asks for an investigation into "private financial benefit, preferential treatment, or access" tied to presidential family relationships.

  • Curtis wants the committee to subpoena both sons to testify about "any instances in which their relationship to the President was invoked or understood to provide value."

"The latest: Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), who lost his GOP primary earlier this year after Trump endorsed his opponent, said Tuesday he would support Curtis' request." After "Driving the news.

Catch up quick: ProPublica reported that Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev paid hundreds of thousands of dollars toward Trump Jr.'s three-day wedding celebration in the Bahamas, including buying a private-island rental.

  • Curtis also cited Trump Jr.'s ties to prediction markets. Trump Jr. is a paid strategic adviser to Kalshi and sits on Polymarket's advisory board. 1789 Capital, where Trump Jr. is a partner, has invested in Polymarket.
  • Curtis also pointed to Trump family-backed cryptocurrency ventures, international real estate deals involving meetings with foreign heads of state, and Trump Jr.'s reported defense-sector investments.

What he's saying: "A toaster is a wedding gift," Curtis wrote on X. "A private-island party paid for by a Putin-connected oligarch is something else. Republicans nearly wore out the subpoena machine investigating Hunter Biden's foreign relationships. We should not unplug it now. 'Trust us' was not enough then, and it is not enough now."

For the record: The White House, Trump Jr. and Hunter Biden have not yet responded to requests for comment.

  • Hunter Biden has denied involving his father in business dealings.
  • Trump Jr. confirmed Kremlev hosted celebrations, describing it as a wedding gift from a friend. President Trump later defended the arrangement as "totally allowed" and said he had been told his son would repay Kremlev.

Flashback: House Republicans subpoenaed Hunter Biden in 2023 as part of their impeachment inquiry into then-President Biden.

  • The younger Biden testified that he did not involve his father in his business dealings.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from Sen. John Cornyn.

item.title: Trump backs ban on diesel exports
item.description:
President Trump said Tuesday that he has called for a ban on U.S. diesel exports, while Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed the administration is examining whether a full or partial ban is feasible.

Why it matters: Trump's endorsement marks a shift for an administration that has resisted calls to restrict fuel exports, as record diesel prices squeeze farmers and truckers and fuel Republican concerns ahead of the midterms.

  • Economists and energy analysts the move could lower diesel prices for Americans in the short term but would likely raise prices globally including eventually in the U.S.

Zoom in: When asked during a press briefing alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky if he supported a diesel ban endorsed by other Republicans, Trump said that he had called for that too.

  • "I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel, and it could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, you know it's a sort of a flow, it's a balance. But no, I've called for it. I've called for it within my people."
  • Bessent, sitting beside Trump, said the administration was examining "whether it's feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity, and whether a full or a partial ban would work."
  • When asked about the timeline of such a decision, Trump replied: "Fast, one way or the other."

Catch up quick: Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) recently proposed blocking diesel exports, hoping to lower prices domestically, and other farm-state Republicans quickly signed on too.

  • Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who faces a competitive re-election race, called for a diesel ban Monday while slamming the war in Iran. Republicans in Michigan and Louisiana did the same.
  • Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said last week that he was "open" to an export ban.

Zoom in: A ban would keep diesel that otherwise would be exported in the U.S., potentially increasing domestic supplies and lowering prices in the short term.

  • But analysts warn it could drive up global diesel prices and eventually feed higher costs back into the U.S. economy.
  • The U.S. has rarely resorted to outright energy export bans because of concerns about disrupting global markets.

Flashback: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said last week the administration would consider an export ban if it would lower prices, "but that's not the case."

💭 Thought bubble, via Axios Future of Energy co-author Ben Geman: The politics of $6.50 diesel are quickly overwhelming a broad consensus among oil market analysts that an export ban could ultimately backfire.

Zoom out: Trump does have emergency powers that could allow him to enforce a ban.

  • Congress could also pass legislation to achieve the same goal, but Senate Republicans are significantly divided on the measure.
  • Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) questioned whether a ban was worth rocking global markets, calling it a "short-term" benefit … "that doesn't really move the needle."
  • Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) called it "a gimmick."

What they're saying: American Petroleum Institute CEO Mike Sommers said restricting U.S. energy exports would "only compound the problem," exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers.

  • "The answer is more supply and more flexibility — not new restrictions that risk making a difficult situation worse," Sommers said.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout.

Ben Geman contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump TV is live. Here's what it's actually showing
item.description:
As President Trump fights the press over coverage, the White House launched its own 24/7 streaming channel — Trump TV.

Why it matters: Trump TV gives the president a White House-run video platform to reach the public without relying on traditional news organizations.

  • So far, Trump TV resembles a round-the-clock presidential highlight reel more than a news network.

Driving the news: Trump TV launched the same day major TV networks suspended White House pool coverage — a protest that left one Trump speech airing without sound.

  • The White House had teased the channel through cryptic videos, and it went live on its YouTube account, WhiteHouse.gov and the official White House app.

Reality check: Presidents have long used White House platforms to share speeches and events with the public.

What we know about Trump TV

How it works: The channel launched as "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station."

  • "Trump TV is a 24/7 livestream of the Administration's greatest hits, unfiltered," Kaelan Dorr, deputy assistant to the president, wrote on X.
  • So far, the channel has shown curated clips of past Trump speeches and executive actions, along with live events.

Catch up quick: The initial programming included Trump's July 3 Mount Rushmore speech before shifting into footage of his 2025 inauguration, per multiple reports.

  • The Daily Beast reports 8,500 viewers were watching the stream during its first hour.
  • Around 1,200 people were watching Tuesday afternoon as the channel aired a Trump health care announcement from August, according to an Axios review of the stream.

Zoom in: The stream can also carry live events.

  • On Tuesday, the stream carried Vice President Vance's briefing on fraud claims.
  • But while Trump addressed the United Nations General Assembly Tuesday morning, Trump TV was replaying an earlier speech from the National Prayer Breakfast.

Unanswered questions about Trump TV

What we're watching: So far, Trump TV has no anchors, news ticker or headline chyrons.

  • The stream includes banners asking viewers to text White House officials.
  • It's unclear who staffs the channel, makes programming decisions or sets its schedule.

What they're saying: A White House official tells Axios that the channel's purpose is to replay Trump's "greatest hits that the media fails to cover fairly, oftentimes on purpose."

The intrigue: The White House's revamped livestream page labels its regular feed "CH 45" and Trump TV "CH 47" — references to Trump serving as the 45th and 47th president.

Trump's previous streaming ventures

Flashback: Trump has experimented with direct-to-audience video before.

  • In 2016, Trump's presidential campaign launched a nightly Facebook Live show called "Trump Tower Live" that was meant to deliver campaign messaging directly to the public.

Trump Media's Truth+ offers 24/7 news streams and on-demand entertainment.

  • It appears on Truth+ apps and remains a commercial streaming service rather than an official government stream.
  • The service began rolling out in 2024. Its lineup has included broadcasts of Newsmax, OAN and Real America's Voice.

item.title: Cheap, powerful AI models are increasing usage, a bullish sign for the AI boom
item.description:
AI companies have competed on having the best and often most dangerous models for years. Now, they're pivoting to a new focus: cost.

Why it matters: The biggest risk to the AI boom is demand, and recent innovations to make models cheaper while maintaining powerful levels of intelligence have offered a bullish signal.

  • As the prices of top models from OpenAI, Anthropic and others come down, usage is increasing dramatically, a trend that points to the kind of demand that will be necessary to justify trillions of dollars in spending.

State of play: It's modelpalooza in the AI world this week, with OpenAI, Anthropic, SpaceX and some Chinese model providers all offering new releases. Most of them are offering shocking levels of intelligence at prices that would've been unthinkable just a few months ago.

  • OpenAI is releasing GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on Tuesday, which bring down the cost for top business customers by 50% from previous iterations of the same models, the company shared with Axios.
  • Anthropic is releasing Opus 5.5 on Tuesday, which the company says costs around 40% less to run than Opus 5 while maintaining top intelligence.
  • Elon Musk's xAI on Monday released Grok 4.7, pitching the new model around price-performance. Yet in a testament to the sheer brutality of competition in the AI race, it only took 24 hours for new options to wipe out much of that price advantage.

Threat level: The ferocity and speed of the race during an ongoing price war is an issue for OpenAI and Anthropic, which need to retain customers and revenue growth to justify their sky-high multitrillion-dollar valuations.

Yes, but: Even as they face margin pressure, the trend is positive for the AI boom overall, as the price reductions make it much easier to bet on a bright future for AI use.

Follow the money: There is emerging evidence that cost cutting is a rising tide that can lift revenues for all AI providers.

  • In a report sent to clients, Citadel Securities found that falling per-token costs are fueling additional usage, and overall AI spending is increasing. That points to higher eventual profits for labs or any company providing the computing firepower that services AI usage.
  • Morgan Stanley sees competition from Chinese providers as yet another bullish signal for AI because it will increase overall demand for computing by capturing more customers who can now access AI for less.
  • This concept is referred to in classic economic theory as Jevons paradox, which holds that when technology brings down the cost of a resource, consumption increases.

Between the lines: Open-weight model companies, primarily coming out of China, have been on a tear in recent weeks.

  • DeepSeek this month released V4.1 Flash, which it says beats its previous flagship offering on a number of benchmarks with technical updates that allow the company to charge less for its intelligence.
  • That model is now No. 1 on OpenRouter's leaderboard with a 172% spike in usage this week.

Reality check: Lowering costs to take market share isn't new in the AI world.

  • AI companies have a long history of releasing a new model and then lowering the cost for prior releases, or even releasing "flash" versions of larger models that are smaller and cheaper to run.
  • But the increased competition from open-weight model providers and their massive rise on leaderboards is fueling a broader focus on cost across offerings from top AI labs.

The bottom line: AI sticker shock feels like a distant memory given the massive push from labs to deliver cheaper models.

item.title: Exclusive: Trump adviser ties high gas prices to refining
item.description:
The affordability of gasoline remains "the top issue that the president looks at," Trump energy adviser Jarrod Agen said at an Axios House event Tuesday.

Why it matters: The Trump administration is championing energy savings from its deregulatory push as overseas conflicts, including the Iran war, rattle oil markets, driving up fuel costs and threatening an expensive winter for millions of households.

  • Tuesday's national average gas price was roughly $4.48, up from around $3.18 a year ago, per AAA.

Driving the news: Asked by Axios' Amy Harder if the president takes responsibility for the higher prices Americans are paying, Agen said that the president's "long-term goal is preventing Iran" from having "nuclear capabilities."

  • "He says the long term is worth it to stop them from having a nuclear weapon."

Flashback: Asked last year what a successful term would look like once the administration's time in Washington is up, Agen told Axios' Mike Allen that the one factor the president always looks at is the price at the pump.

  • "We want to make sure that U.S. consumers are paying not high prices on their electricity bills and gas," he said. "That is the key that ... drives us every single day."

Zoom in: Pressed on those remarks, Agen told Harder it's "still the top issue the president looks at" and attributed the price pain to strained refining capacity.

  • "We've got crude flowing," he said, though the full picture of how much oil is leaving the Strait of Hormuz isn't yet entirely clear.
  • "More crude is on the market, and so that's great. But refining capacity is the issue we're trying to solve, both domestically and then globally," Agen said. "If you look at refining capacity, Russia, for example, it's down 30, 40% China is not at their capacity."
  • He floated the possibility of relief via the Defense Production Act, which Trump already invoked, and infrastructure projects "to attack the refining issue."

Catch up quick: The national average diesel price shattered its record earlier this month and then topped $6 a gallon for the first time, threatening higher inflation and household costs amid already elevated fuel prices.

  • An estimate from Brown University found that the war in Iran has cost U.S. consumers more than $100 billion in higher energy prices, adding to the administration's affordability challenges ahead of the midterms as Republicans fight to retain control of Congress.
  • Disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and other compounding crises have put American refineries operating near maximum capacity to an unprecedented test and raised questions about whether the administration would place an export ban on American diesel.

What he's saying: Trump addressed the General Assembly gathering Tuesday, teling fellow world leaders that he "gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran."

Go deeper: Gas prices are rising again — and so is GOP grief in the midterms

item.title: Love is pricey. Here's what young Americans are doing about it
item.description:
Data: Zelle New Economics of Dating Report; Chart: Avery Lotz/Axios

Rising costs are changing dating for more than eight in 10 Gen Z and millennial daters, leaving some to stop courting altogether, per new data from Zelle.

The big picture: Young Americans are pushing off milestones under cost pressures — and the milestones themselves, from getting hitched to buying a home, are getting pricier once they get there.

Driving the news: For younger Americans, just planning a date is a costly ordeal, with 17% of active Gen Z and Millennial daters saying they've gone into debt trying to maintain the dating lifestyle.

  • Nearly one-third say they've gone on fewer dates amid rising costs. A smaller share, 11%, say they've stopped dating because they couldn't afford it.
  • Members of Gen Z are more likely to split the cost of a date because of rising costs (26%) than Millennials (18%).
  • Daters have changed strategies to lighten the cost burden — like suggesting free activities and spending more time on dates at home, which were used by 37% and 33% of active daters, respectively.

The intrigue: As costs weigh on younger Americans, perhaps it's unsurprising that checkbook chemistry plays a big role in their love stories: Half of active daters say financial compatibility has at some point mattered more than romantic chemistry when deciding to keep dating someone.

  • Men are more likely to say that than women (56% versus 45%), as are Gen Zers (53%) than Millennials (46%).
  • But be warned: Talking money too much can kill the mood. For example, complaining about the price of everything or chatting too much about income would both give 47% of daters the "ick."

What they're saying: "Dating has always come with unspoken rules, but rising costs are forcing a rewrite," Denise Leonhard, general manager of Zelle, said in a statement.

  •  "Financial compatibility is becoming part of the chemistry test. The new flex isn't running up the tab; it's reading the room, respecting the budget and showing thought."

Zoom out: It comes as nearly all younger Americans (96%) reported being concerned about the cost of rent, groceries, gas or utilities, according to a recent Axios-Generation Lab poll of 18- to 34-year-olds.

  • With the Game of Life ahead of them, high costs are leaving younger Americans struggling to even get on the board.

Methodology: This online survey of 1,800 U.S. adults ages 18 and older was fielded August 14–25. Statistical testing is reported at the 95% confidence level.

Go deeper: Youth poll: Thumbs down on everything

  • With the Game of Life ahead of them, high costs are leaving younger Americans struggling to even get on the board.

Methodology: This online survey of 1,800 U.S. adults ages 18 and older was fielded August 14–25. Statistical testing is reported at the 95% confidence level.

item.title: The AI doomsday fear hidden in self-improving AI
item.description:
Of the various ways experts fear AI could kill us all, one is slowly moving closer to reality: AI learning to make itself unstoppable.

Why it matters: Recursive self-improvement, the ability of an AI model to build better versions of itself without human guidance, could make increasingly capable systems harder for humans to control.

  • The RSI threshold doesn't represent danger by itself, but a lack of human control combined with rogue AI agents is a scenario that safety-conscious AI researchers have long feared.

Driving the news: Researchers at Anthropic and OpenAI say the process of training new models has grown more automated, coming close to the RSI rubicon.

  • An OpenAI employee told The Information the company has largely automated training new experimental models, with AI systems running experiments as directed by humans and correcting much of their work.
  • Last week, Anthropic shared that its AI training is becoming more automated, with AI leading about 26% of Anthropic's R&D work. AI collaborates on 90% of work, the company says.
  • "AI systems are getting more powerful, and they're increasingly being used to build the next version of themselves," the company said.

Reality check: Critics say the milestone is more a function of coding automation than a marker of impending doom or inevitable AI superpowers.

  • While there's been an uptick in troubling AI security incidents in which models outstripped human control, some industry figures see those episodes as evidence of poor internal controls by OpenAI and other companies.
  • Further evidence of that view emerged this week, when the Wall Street Journal reported that independent security researchers used Anthropic's Claude to break into OpenAI in July.

Where does RSI come from?

Flashback: The concept behind RSI emerged in the 1950s as artificial intelligence became an area of study.

  • British mathematician and statistician Irving John Good described the idea in a 1965 paper: "Thus the first ultraintelligent machine is the last invention that man need ever make, provided that the machine is docile enough to tell us how to keep it under control."

How RSI could lead to AI doom

Threat level: Anthropic has warned RSI "might increase the risks of humans losing control over AI systems."

  • Some researchers theorize that advanced AI could resist shutdown or modification if staying operational helped it accomplish its goals.
  • Researchers into the hack by OpenAI agents into Hugging Face said the agents showed signs of this behavior.

Another concern: Self-improving AI systems capable of copying themselves could create a kind of digital natural selection, favoring systems that are best at acquiring compute, money and power to grow fastest.

  • In a darker version of this scenario, AI would be competing with humans for resources and power, experts say.

Between the lines: Dangerous behavior might not stop with one generation of AI.

  • Anthropic researchers found that some unwanted traits could pass from one model to another through training data, raising concerns that problematic behavior could persist across generations of AI.

How close are we to RSI?

The big picture: We're not there yet. A new analysis published this week found that AI feedback loops aren't yet hitting the RSI benchmarks.

What we're watching: Attempts at building RSI.

  • China's z.AI says they're heading toward RSI, where the models are helping build better infrastructure for better models.
  • Google DeepMind researchers published a framework for "Dream-RSI," a system that recursively improves how an AI agent finds solutions.

The bottom line: RSI isn't here yet, but it's a looming issue that's got the AI world on watch.

Go deeper: AI's architects say the next era of human history is here
