item.title: Trump bans CNN, MS NOW and Politico from White House
item.description:
President Trump said Friday he is banning CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House "effective immediately," escalating his long-running battles with news organizations.

  • Early Saturday morning, Politico, CNN and MS NOW said their journalists were denied access to White House grounds.

Why it matters: Trump is seeking to use White House access against news outlets whose coverage he objects to, while threatening to target additional organizations.

  • Press freedom groups immediately called on news outlets to fight the bans.

Driving the news: Trump's Truth Social post called the three outlets "Fake News" and accused them of reporting "FICTION and LIES," before threatening to also ban other "Fake News Media Outlets."

  • The White House declined to comment beyond Trump's post.
  • "CNN stands fully behind our White House team and their fair and accurate reporting," the network posted on X. "We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do that reporting without hindrance or interference from the government. Should the ban which President Trump threatened go ahead, it would be an illegal assault on that fundamental and constitutionally-protected right."
  • Politico similarly wrote that it "will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them."

Between the lines: The scope of the ban wasn't immediately clear. As of shortly after the post, CNN continued to work from the White House, the network reported.

  • But Saturday morning journalists for CNN, MS NOW and Politico were unable to gain access. "MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy," the network said in a statement.
  • The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals has previously held that once the White House opens general press facilities to journalists, access can't be denied arbitrarily, and press pass restrictions must come with due process.
  • A divided appellate court last year said the White House does have broader discretion over which journalists enter restricted spaces like the Oval Office and Air Force One. That case, brought by the Associated Press, remains unresolved.

Friction point: Trump has previously moved to restrict access for reporters and outlets he has clashed with.

  • In 2018, the White House revoked CNN reporter Jim Acosta's credential. A federal judge later ordered the pass restored.
  • Last year, the administration barred the AP from some events because it continued to use "Gulf of Mexico," sparking the still-pending First Amendment case.

State of play: The White House took control of selecting the presidential press pool from the White House Correspondents' Association last year.

  • The Pentagon has also restricted press access, but a federal judge this year struck down parts of its credentialing policy. The Defense Department responded with a different restrictive policy that was also blocked, though that decision has been stayed pending appeal.
  • Last month, the Treasury Department denied credentials to some journalists who sought to cover the G20 meeting in North Carolina.

What they're saying: Press freedom groups raised alarms about Trump's announced ban.

  • Seth Stern, Freedom of the Press Foundation's advocacy director, called banning outlets over their coverage "a blatant violation of the First Amendment" and urged news outlets to challenge restrictions.
  • Jameel Jaffer, executive director of the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, compared the move to Trump's efforts targeting universities and law firms.
  • "With so many courts having ruled against him on exactly this point, you'd think President Trump would have learned this lesson by now," Jaffer said in a statement.
  • The National Press Club blasted the move as well. "Every American should understand what is at stake. If implemented, this ban would mark an unprecedented assault on press freedom," president Mark Schoeff Jr. said in a statement.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer likened Trump's actions to those of an autocrat.

  • "Donald Trump just did what dictators throughout history have done," Schumer wrote on X. "@realDonaldTrump- this is a democracy. You will not be able to manipulate the news or hide the truth."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with new information throughout.

item.title: Iran war causes global pain at the pump
item.description:
Data: Axios research. Note: Some countries use a quota system for gasoline. Malaysia's figure reflects the unsubsidized market rate. Chart: Noah Bressner/Axios

The Iran war is driving fuel prices higher worldwide, leading to angry protests around the globe and straining the economies of countries that have nothing to do with the war.

Why it matters: It's not just driving up prices in the U.S. The war is causing problems around the world — in some cases far worse than anything Americans are experiencing.

  • The surge in prices squeezes consumers, and worsens the finances of governments trying to contain the shock — especially poorer and developing countries with little fiscal running room.
  • It affects many nations that are also facing higher prices for natural gas, diesel and other fuels.

Zoom out: The map above, based on World Bank data, shows the upward global trend.

Yes, but: Price increases vary greatly from country to country.

  • A number of countries that are heavily reliant on fuel imports, like Pakistan and Myanmar, have seen steep price hikes.
  • But the U.S., the world's largest oil and gasoline producer, also has soaring prices.
  • Crude oil prices, the biggest input into gasoline costs, are set on global markets. The U.S. federal government, unlike some nations, has not set caps or subsidies on retail prices.

Context: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries are also helping to boost motor fuel prices, especially diesel.

The big picture: With no resolution to the conflict in sight, many governments face hard choices — strain their budgets with fuel support or face the political consequences of higher fuel costs.

State of play: Dozens of nations have taken steps to cap, subsidize or lower taxes on various fuels, per the International Energy Agency. Governments are also taking steps to reduce demand, such as more remote work and limiting government travel.

  • The International Monetary Fund is worried about the fiscal hit from price supports, especially if they outlast the energy shock.
  • "[A] large share of measures described as temporary lack clear expiration dates or fiscal cost estimates," senior IMF officials wrote over the summer.

What they're saying: "Many places have failed to reduce demand and are instead artificially constraining prices," said Joseph Webster, an energy scholar with the Atlantic Council.

  • "This approach is misguided: gradual, managed demand reduction is far less politically damaging than sudden, sharp, and chaotic rationing," he said via email.
  • He also said countries should taper withdrawal of subsidies, because allowing prices to soar overnight can bring unrest.

Zoom in: Rising fuel costs are compounding existing inflation, public debt and youth unemployment problems in Kenya, Carnegie Endowment for International Peace scholars wrote in late August.

  • It's also among the nations slammed with higher fertilizer costs as a result of the war.
  • The country, which relies heavily on Middle East fuel imports, had major protests in May, and its problems are not unique.

"Kenya's case serves as a signal for others in the region caught downstream of the war's economic blow," they write, arguing for greater "resilience" measures that make nations less vulnerable to external shocks.

item.title: Football drives GOP's TV ad blitz for the midterms
item.description:
Republicans scrambling for midterm momentum are making a massive bet on football, pouring millions into advertising during the country's biggest NFL and college games.

Why it matters: Across the country, Republicans are trying to hold onto male voters — football's core audience and a critical part of President Trump's 2024 coalition.

  • After winning 55% of the male vote in 2024, Trump has seen his standing with men deteriorate. A new Fox News poll puts his approval among them at 42%, down 9 points from a year ago.
  • The signs of slippage are particularly clear among young men. A spring Harvard Youth Poll found men ages 18–29 favored a Democratic congressional candidate by 8 points, after reporting an even split between Trump and Harris in 2024.

By the numbers: Part of Republicans' plan to try to change the midterm vibe is to capitalize on their financial advantage by dominating the football airwaves.

  • They ran 5,546 TV spots during the NFL and college games and pre-and-postgame programming where they advertised most heavily last weekend, compared with 471 for Democrats — nearly 12 times as many, according to ad-tracking data obtained by Axios.
  • Republicans' biggest presence was during the blockbuster Texas-Ohio State matchup, which featured teams from two states with competitive Senate races.
  • The pro-GOP Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) super PAC spent $2 million, airing ads in every quarter before 14 million viewers on ABC.
  • The national coverage meant viewers nationwide saw Senate ads that were targeted to Texas or Ohio.

Zoom in: Nowhere is the GOP's football strategy more apparent than in Michigan, where the Senate race could determine control of that chamber.

  • SLF struck a deal with a vendor that manages sports programming in Michigan bars, putting its ads on more than 1,000 TVs at 150 bars across the state.
  • Republicans launched the effort after Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed made critical remarks about football, which became the focus of the ads.
  • A super PAC supporting Republican Mike Rogers premiered its latest ad attacking El-Sayed during Thursday night's Lions-Bills game and will air it again during Saturday's Michigan State-Notre Dame game on NBC.

Zoom out: The push extends beyond advertising.

  • Turning Point USA, the conservative group once led by Charlie Kirk, launched "Grand American Tailgate," a get-out-the-vote tour of college campuses on football Saturdays. This weekend it heads to Oxford, Miss., ahead of the Ole Miss-LSU game.
  • Minnesota Senate candidate Michelle Tafoya is spotlighting her career as an NFL sideline reporter, while Arizona House candidate and former NFL kicker Jay Feely highlighted his football career during his speech at the GOP's midterm convention.
  • Rogers campaigned at last weekend's Michigan-Oklahoma game in Ann Arbor and gave an interview outside Michigan Stadium — the "Big House" — noting that his dad had been a high school coach.

The White House is joining in with football-themed social posts, including one showing Trump dancing to Fox's NFL theme.

Flashback: In 2024, Republicans spent millions on ads during football games attacking Kamala Harris over transgender issues, including transgender women participating in women's sports.

  • Trump advisers credited the ads with helping him make inroads with young men. The presidential margin among men under 50 swung 11 points toward Trump between 2020 and 2024, according to Pew Research.
  • Republicans are reviving the strategy. The pro-GOP Congressional Leadership Fund ran two ads during last weekend's Iowa-Iowa State game, including one attacking a Democratic candidate on transgender issues.
  • Texas Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, who faces Democrat James Talarico in November, is airing ads on the same issue during NFL games.

Yes, but: Democrats aren't abandoning football. Talarico will advertise during Sunday's Dallas Cowboys-Washington Commanders NFL game, for which a 30-second candidate spot costs $200,000, according to the ad buying company Medium Buying.

What they're saying: Republicans say football's enormous reach is worth the price.

  • "Smart campaigns and organizations recognize that live sports remain one of the last few remaining shared cultural events where millions of Americans watch live," SLF Political Director Domenic Re told Axios.

item.title: Google is the latest AI lab with a security testing mishap
item.description:
Google's Gemini AI model broke into three companies' systems using basic hacking techniques during model testing earlier this year.

Why it matters: Google was one of the only AI labs that hadn't yet publicly disclosed a security breach involving their agents during routine pre-deployment testing.

Driving the news: Google confirmed the three incidents, which happened in May, on Friday.

  • The incidents happened as part of a test run that third-party evaluator Irregular was operating — similar to other security breaches involving OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta's AI models.
  • The Wall Street Journal first reported the incidents.

What they're saying: "Safe development of powerful AI models is critical and we invest deeply in this area," Heather Adkins, vice president of security engineering at Google, said in a statement.

  • Adkins added that her team contacted the affected entities and "worked with our training partner on the changes they've now made to their testing processes."
  • An Irregular spokesperson confirmed to Axios that the Gemini incident involved the same security issues that also led to similar incidents involving other AI labs' models.
  • The spokesperson also said in a statement all "relevant labs were notified in late July" and that "all known issues on our end were remedied and resolved weeks ago."

Zoom in: The hacks happened while Gemini was completing a "capture the flag" hacking exercise, where the model was asked to retrieve information from software operated by a fictional company inside a testing environment, per the WSJ.

  • However, the fictional company had the same name as a real one.
  • In one case, the model guessed passwords for a protected system until it gained access. In the other two cases, the model found credentials in a public repository that then allowed it to access other protected systems.

Yes, but: Google's model stopped their actions as soon as they realized they accessed real companies.

The intrigue: Irregular told the Wall Street Journal that the model wasn't supposed to be able to get online, but internet access was unintentionally available.

  • After OpenAI and Anthropic disclosed additional incidents this summer, a source familiar with the matter told Axios that the AI labs and Irregular weren't fully aligned on the exact testing procedures and safeguards, leaving ambiguities in how each side expected the typically internet-enabled evaluations to run.

Go deeper: Researchers playing rogue AI agent hide-and-seek on the open web

item.title: DOJ won't enforce handgun ban for 18- to 20-year-olds
item.description:
The Justice Department said Friday it will not criminally enforce a 1968 federal law barring licensed gun dealers from selling handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds, after its Office of Legal Counsel concluded the restriction violated the Second Amendment.

Why it matters: The Trump administration is telling federal prosecutors not to enforce a law passed by Congress, even though the Supreme Court has never ruled on its constitutionality.

  • The decision could give adults under the age of 21 access to the country's licensed handgun market, though it remains unclear whether dealers will begin selling to them immediately.

The latest: The Thursday opinion signed by Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser stands as controlling legal advice for the executive branch, though it isn't a court ruling and doesn't bind judges or erase the law.

  • Gaiser wrote that 18- to 20-year-olds are adults protected by the Second Amendment, and the right to own handguns includes the ability to buy them.
  • While the opinion said criminal enforcement was unconstitutional, it didn't address whether agencies like the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives could continue administrative enforcement of the ban.
  • The White House, the Department of Justice, and ATF have not yet responded to Axios' requests for comment.

The other side: Giffords, a gun-safety advocacy group, called the move "illegal and dangerous" and said it would "do everything we can to fight this."

  • Kris Brown, president of Brady: United Against Gun Violence, said the opinion "does not change the law itself" and misreads the nation's history of gun regulation.
  • "The provision prohibiting the sale of handguns to 18-to-20-year-olds has protected public safety for generations," Brown said in a statement. "This opinion by the Department of Justice is yet more evidence that the Trump administration is prioritizing the gun industry's wishlist, rather than protecting American lives."

State of play: The Supreme Court has denied petitions asking it to decide the constitutionality of state and federal bans for adults younger than 21.

  • Federal appellate circuits remain split on whether age restrictions like this can stand. Three have struck down restrictions, while three others have upheld them.
  • The Supreme Court's 2022 Bruen decision upended how courts judge gun restrictions, requiring any regulations be consistent with the country's historical tradition of firearm regulation.

What they're saying: Firearms Policy Coalition, one of the plaintiffs challenging the same restriction in an active case, said the "federal government cannot justify denying [18- to 20-year-olds] access to handguns based solely on age."

  • The gun-rights advocacy group said while it agrees with the opinion's rationale, it wants the DOJ to go further, including covering handgun ammunition.

Reality check: The group isn't yet telling licensed dealers they can begin making the sales.

  • "ATF's currently published dealer guidance still reflects the age restriction, so we are reviewing how ATF implements the opinion before giving broader guidance."
  • Other federal requirements and state laws also still apply, FPC said.

The big picture: The move is part of President Trump's broader effort to reshape gun policy.

  • Trump ordered then-Attorney General Pam Bondi to examine regulations, enforcement and litigation for potential infringements of Second Amendment rights.
  • After OLC concluded in January that a nearly century-old ban on mailing handguns was unconstitutional, the Postal Service proposed allowing lawful handguns to be mailed under the same conditions as rifles and shotguns.
  • Federal agencies have scrapped enforcement policies and proposed new rules that gun-rights groups have long asked for.

The Justice Department said Friday it will not criminally enforce a 1968 federal law barring licensed gun dealers from selling handguns to 18- to 20-year-olds, after its Office of Legal Counsel concluded the restriction violated the Second Amendment.

Why it matters: The Trump administration is telling federal prosecutors not to enforce a law passed by Congress, even though the Supreme Court has never ruled on its constitutionality.

  • The decision could give adults under the age of 21 access to the country's licensed handgun market, though it remains unclear whether dealers will begin selling to them immediately.

The latest: The Thursday opinion signed by Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser stands as controlling legal advice for the executive branch, though it isn't a court ruling and doesn't bind judges or erase the law.

  • Gaiser wrote that 18- to 20-year-olds are adults protected by the Second Amendment, and the right to own handguns includes the ability to buy them.
  • While the opinion said criminal enforcement was unconstitutional, it didn't address whether agencies like the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives could continue administrative enforcement of the ban.

item.title: Trump claims security, military deal with Denmark over Greenland
item.description:
President Trump said late Friday the U.S. has struck a deal with Denmark that will give America "permanent control over security" in Greenland.

Why it matters: Control over Greenland has been a fixation of Trump's for years and a wedge in U.S. relations with Europe.

  • Any such deal could potentially reduce tensions with the EU, though it's unclear how residents of the island itself will take to the pact.

What they're saying: "I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland, completely addressing ALL of our many U.S. concerns," Trump posted on Truth Social.

  • "There will be NO COST to the United States!"

The other side: The office of Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said the three parties would sign the "great agreement" in New York next week at the UN General Assembly, adding that it was a good deal for NATO and Europe as well.

  • "The agreement recognizes Greenland's interests and our place in the international cooperation. It is to the benefit of us all," Greenland Premier Jens-Frederik Nielsen said in a statement.

Between the lines: Trump said in his post that the U.S. will build a large military presence on the island, though he did not specify where or how large.

  • He also indicated the U.S. would have a veto over other countries having military bases or sensitive investments on the island.
  • Fox News, citing an unnamed U.S. official, said the deal stops short of full sovereignty over Greenland, but is designed to persist even if the island becomes an independent nation someday.

Context: Danish and Greenlandic leaders have consistently told Trump that Greenland is not for sale.

  • Under a 1951 defense agreement with Denmark, the U.S. already has military access to the island. But Trump has repeatedly claimed that the U.S. needs Greenland.
  • Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte discussed a Greenland framework in January that briefly abated talk of the U.S. annexing the island.
  • However, Trump's desire to annex new land has come up repeatedly during his second term.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with statements from Denmark and Greenland

item.title: USPS made mail slower to cut costs. Midterm ballots will test the system.
item.description:
The U.S. Postal Service has slowed down mail deliveries so much it's failing to meet even its lowered performance targets, a new report from the Government Accountability Office found.

Why it matters: The Postal Service is part of the connective tissue of American life: delivering prescription drugs and ballots, carrying government notices and bills, helping businesses reach customers across the country.

  • Now its attempts to shore up its finances are disproportionately affecting rural communities.

The big picture: The Postal Service has given itself more time to deliver some first-class mail, the congressional watchdog's report notes, which millions of Americans rely on for medications, bills, paychecks, financial documents and mail-in ballots.

  • The USPS is expected to fund itself largely through postage and other revenue while also providing universal service to nearly every U.S. address, even where doing so isn't profitable.

By the numbers: The USPS added one to two days to expected delivery times for some mail after shifting some transportation from air to ground in 2021.

  • The report said about 24,000 post offices will lose afternoon mail collection if they're more than 50 miles from a regional processing and delivery center, disproportionately affecting rural Americans.

The intrigue: The service concerns come just weeks before the midterms, when millions of voters will rely on USPS to return ballots under state-specific deadlines.

  • The Trump administration has pushed to dramatically overhaul the country's mail-in ballot system.

What they're saying: "Whenever the post office closes … for rural communities, that takes the heart out of the place," Steve Hutkins, editor of Save the Post Office, tells Axios.

  • "Everybody talks about how slow the mail is now. … The goalposts have moved several times," he said, adding that delivery times have slowed four times since 2010. "It all adds up."
  • "The problem is if you want to cut costs to try to balance the books, you're going to cut services one way or another, and services usually means how fast the mail is moving, or whether there's a post office in your town."

Case in point: Residents of one Phoenix neighborhood told Axios they sometimes went days or weeks without mail, leading to missed bills, checks and wedding invitations.

Zoom in: Mark Jamison, a former postmaster in a small North Carolina town, tells Axios, says the decades-long push to operate the Post Office like a business has come at the expense of delivery service.

  • "[I]n the age of ecommerce," he said, the Postal service acts "as a hedge against the delivery monopolies of UPS, FedEx, and Amazon."
  • "The failure to understand the postal system as an essential infrastructure while trying to cram it into an ill-fitting, profit oriented, corporate model has caused serious damage to the infrastructure and been a great disservice to the American people."

The other side: A USPS spokesperson pointed Axios to the agency's comments in the GAO report.

  • "The Postal Service is well positioned to close the fiscal year strong, meet our higher target for first class mail on-time performance, and enter FY27 with significant momentum to set us up for a strong holiday mailing and shipping season."

What we're watching: The GAO recommended the postmaster general explain how the agency plans to improve in its 2027 strategic plan update — and the office agreed.

Go deeper: USPS whistleblower warns new ballot system could fail

item.title: 2028 Democrats like Newsom and Pritzker lean in on AI safety as Washington stalls
item.description:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a presumptive presidential candidate, is getting louder on AI, releasing an executive order amid the Washington stalemate.

Why it matters: Democrats with national profiles this week are seizing on AI alarm, making their positions clear and Newsom – despite some deference shown to other 2028 contender Kamala Harris – wasn't going to sit this one out.

Driving the news: Newsom on Friday issued an executive order tackling two major topics of debate inside the beltway this week -- independent auditors and kill switches.

  • He did so taking direct aim at Washington: "With Donald Trump and Congress asleep at the wheel, Governor Gavin Newsom is once again taking the lead to strengthen AI safety for all Americans."
  • Newsom was early to stake out a position on an issue that is increasingly politically salient, signing the first AI executive order in 2023.

Between the lines: In the absence of U.S. legislation or more action from the Trump administration, states have stepped in to fill the void on AI regulation, a development some top AI execs sought to avoid.

  • There are more than 600 bills in 47 states about AI, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures, up 24% from last year.
  • California, Illinois and Massachusetts are among the states leading the charge. All three are run by Democrats, who are seeking to seize the mantle of AI regulation nationally.

Yes, but: Politicians in both parties are using antipathy toward data centers to punish opponents, including GOP candidates in gubernatorial races in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.

California has emerged as both the state filling the federal regulatory void and one largely aligned with the frontier AI labs it is regulating.

  • The executive order accelerates the implementation of two bills signed into law last week -- both of which were endorsed by OpenAI and Anthropic -- on independent verification organizations.
  • Newsom's position on a kill switch is also aligned with what frontier labs are already working toward.

The big picture: Former Vice President Harris this week also called for slowing down advanced AI development and Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker -- another presidential contender -- on Friday touted his AI bill.

  • "Trump says that the only AI guardrails that we need are a strong and smart president. And, of course, he is neither of those things," Pritzker said.
  • The Illinois bill requires companies to implement their own frameworks for frontier AI safety. A third party then has to create an annual report assessing whether developers are complying with that requirement.

What we're watching: The Senate bill in Massachusetts goes further than Illinois, mandating independent evaluations of the models themselves, every four months.

  • Anthropic has backed it, while OpenAI has backed a narrower version.
  • OpenAI shifted its position on California's bills last week and may do so again in Massachusetts as AI alarm mounts.

item.title: GOP's Latino gains fade as deeper gender and generational divides emerge
item.description:
Latino voters swung sharply toward Republicans in 2024. Now, much of that gain is fading as gender and generational divides widen.

Why it matters: The GOP breakthrough two years ago hasn't produced a uniformly more conservative Latino electorate, as Democrats have regained ground in polling this year.

  • But an Axios analysis of recent polls shows Latino voters aren't simply swinging right, then left. The data show Latino politics fragmenting from within, as young Latino men and women increasingly split over immigration, President Trump and democracy.

By the numbers: Democrats lead Republicans 56%-29% on the generic House ballot among 1,353 Latino registered voters in seven battleground states, according to a new bipartisan BSP Research/Shaw & Co. poll for the American Business Immigration Coalition and American Families United.

  • Among Latino voters, Democrats lead in six states: Arizona, Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Texas.
  • Florida breaks the pattern, with Republicans holding a 44%-43% edge.
  • The pollsters calculated that Democrats' advantage among Latinos is 11 points wider than their Latino margin in 2024.
  • Neither party escapes voter dissatisfaction: 39% view congressional Democrats unfavorably, compared with 63% unfavorably for congressional Republicans.

State of play: Inflation and gas prices remain voters' biggest concerns, but immigration remains highly salient — though voters don't choose between enforcement and legalization as an either-or.

  • 63% called the treatment of immigrants one of their top issues, while 59% said the same about creating legal status for undocumented immigrants with U.S.-citizen family members.
  • 76% preferred a candidate position calling for a bipartisan path to permanent legal status and immigration reform, compared with 24% who preferred a deportation-focused position.

More than 70% in every state surveyed also backed strengthening border security while providing work permits to long-term undocumented immigrants who work and pass a background check.

Zoom in: Some of the sharpest divides now run within generations.

  • Among California Latino registered voters under 30, a new UCLA Latino Policy & Politics Institute analysis of UC Berkeley polling found striking differences between men and women.
  • 88% of young Latinas called protecting immigrant communities very important, versus 60% of young Latino men.
  • 82% of young Latinas called fighting President Trump's agenda very important, versus 52% of young Latino men.
  • On defending democracy and protecting voting rights, 92% of young Latinas called the issue very important, versus 74% of young Latino men.

Zoom out: In the 2024 presidential election, nearly half of Hispanic voters backed Trump — the best performance by a GOP presidential candidate in modern times, according to an Axios review of past elections dating to 1960.

  • But polls show that advantage has been nearly wiped out as Latinos have turned against Trump's moves on immigration, trade and the economy.
  • A Hart Research-TelevisaUnivision poll this month separately found Democrats ahead 58%-35% among 1,500 Latino registered voters in 17 competitive House districts.

What they're saying: "Latino voters are making clear that they don't see border security and legal pathways as competing priorities," Rebecca Shi, executive director of the American Business Immigration Coalition, tells Axios.

  • "Outside the DC bubble, voters aren't one-dimensional: they can want real national security and treating people humanely at the same time," Ashley DeAzevedo, executive director of American Families United, said.

The intrigue: A major Latino evangelical group is stepping into the 2026 election conversation with a message about political disagreement and civic responsibility.

  • The National Latino Evangelical Coalition on Friday released "With Love: A Christian Guide to Faithful Voting," a bilingual, nonpartisan guide asking voters to consider three questions about candidates: whether they demonstrate love of neighbor, show trustworthy character and use power responsibly.
  • "Our responsibility to America and to our neighbors continues long after Election Day," NALEC president Rev. Gabriel Salguero said.

Methodology: The BSP Research/Shaw & Co. poll is based on a survey conducted Sept. 4-16, 2026 of 1,353 Latino registered voters in seven battleground states: Arizona, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Texas.

  • The survey was done in English and Spanish through live telephone interviews, text-message invitations and online panels.
  • The overall margin of error is ±2.7 percentage points.

item.title: The House left town, but Hegseth impeachment, Epstein and a funding fight are waiting
item.description:
House Speaker Mike Johnson has sent lawmakers home until after the midterms, but when they return, they'll quickly face a showdown over impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a renewed Epstein files fight and a looming government funding deadline.

Why it matters: None of these issues will be easy to resolve and could create a headache for the Trump administration in a lame-duck session after Election Day.

Driving the news: Johnson's early seven-week recess sidestepped internal warfare but guaranteed a chaotic stretch of headline-generating fights when lawmakers return.

  • Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced a resolution Tuesday to impeach Hegseth, allowing him to force the House to act on it when lawmakers return.
  • Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) also say they now have enough lawmakers committed to signing a petition to force another vote on files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
  • And government funding expires Dec. 11, giving lawmakers only about a month after they return to resolve another funding fight before the holidays.

Between the lines: The midterms will determine who controls the next Congress.

  • While Republicans remain in charge regardless of election results until Jan. 3, a Democratic-controlled House would end unified Republican control of Washington and gain control of the House agenda.
  • The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

What they're saying: A spokesperson for Johnson referred Axios to his Wednesday comments defending the schedule change so members could "go home to their districts and make their case to the American people."

  • Johnson called the idea the House adjourned to avoid a Hegseth impeachment vote "ridiculous" and dismissed Massie's resolution as a "publicity stunt by someone who wants attention."
  • Hegseth, Johnson said, has "done an extraordinary job."

Yes, but: If Republicans keep the House and Senate, the GOP will be expected to follow through on President Trump's promise to deliver every American adult a $5,000 "Trump Dividend" check.

  • Johnson has said the payments would require congressional approval.
  • The checks would cost an estimated $1.3 trillion amid a $40 trillion national debt.

The bottom line: Johnson's strategy shows how slim majorities make it hard for leadership to control rogue actors and squash unfavorable legislation.

  • Johnson brought temporary relief for vulnerable House Republicans, but did so by trading it for a guaranteed breakneck sprint when the House inevitably returns.

Go deeper: Khanna, Massie say they can force another Epstein vote
item.content:encoded:
House Speaker Mike Johnson has sent lawmakers home until after the midterms, but when they return, they'll quickly face a showdown over impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a renewed Epstein files fight and a looming government funding deadline.

Why it matters: None of these issues will be easy to resolve and could create a headache for the Trump administration in a lame-duck session after Election Day.

Driving the news: Johnson's early seven-week recess sidestepped internal warfare but guaranteed a chaotic stretch of headline-generating fights when lawmakers return.

  • Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) introduced a resolution Tuesday to impeach Hegseth, allowing him to force the House to act on it when lawmakers return.
  • Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) also say they now have enough lawmakers committed to signing a petition to force another vote on files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
  • And government funding expires Dec. 11, giving lawmakers only about a month after they return to resolve another funding fight before the holidays.

Between the lines: The midterms will determine who controls the next Congress.

  • While Republicans remain in charge regardless of election results until Jan. 3, a Democratic-controlled House would end unified Republican control of Washington and gain control of the House agenda.
  • The White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

What they're saying: A spokesperson for Johnson referred Axios to his Wednesday comments defending the schedule change so members could "go home to their districts and make their case to the American people."

  • Johnson called the idea the House adjourned to avoid a Hegseth impeachment vote "ridiculous" and dismissed Massie's resolution as a "publicity stunt by someone who wants attention."
  • Hegseth, Johnson said, has "done an extraordinary job."

Yes, but: If Republicans keep the House and Senate, the GOP will be expected to follow through on President Trump's promise to deliver every American adult a $5,000 "Trump Dividend" check.

  • Johnson has said the payments would require congressional approval.
  • The checks would cost an estimated $1.3 trillion amid a $40 trillion national debt.

The bottom line: Johnson's strategy shows how slim majorities make it hard for leadership to control rogue actors and squash unfavorable legislation.

  • Johnson brought temporary relief for vulnerable House Republicans, but did so by trading it for a guaranteed breakneck sprint when the House inevitably returns.

Go deeper: Khanna, Massie say they can force another Epstein vote

item.title: Khanna, Massie say they can force another Epstein vote
item.description:
Reps. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) announced Thursday they've secured commitments for the 218 signatures needed to force another vote the release of files related to sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The big picture: Answers about the disgraced financier and his web of wealthy connections have continued to haunt the administration, with Attorney General Todd Blanche now facing the threat of contempt proceedings over the Epstein files.

  • This is the bipartisan duo's second push in less than a year after they forced their first Epstein transparency bill through Congress, which the president signed after initially opposing the effort.

Driving the news: "Thomas Massie and I have defied history for a second time," Khanna said in a video posted to social media late Thursday afternoon.

  • His post read that the pair had secured commitments for 218 votes on their discharge petition, including from three Republicans: Reps. Ralph Norman (R-S.C), Nancy Mace (R-S.C.) and Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.).
  • Two Democrats were sick, he added, but will sign the day the House returns. Massie also posted that he and his partner across the aisle would have enough names once lawmakers are back from a lengthy recess.

Friction point: House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) dumped fuel on the fire blazing between him and Massie by again sending the House home early this week, Axios' Kate Santaliz reports.

  • The more than six-week recess will also delay Massie's effort to force a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
  • Johnson's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

What's inside: Massie and Khanna introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II in July to strengthen enforcement of last year's law.

  • It would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the U.S. attorney general over alleged unlawful withholdings, redactions or failure to produce records.
  • The bill would also require the attorney general provide certain unredacted documents to victims upon request.

Flashback: The House voted nearly unanimously on the first transparency act last year.

  • The DOJ released millions of pages related to Epstein — though the information drop faced criticism for puzzling redactions and allegations of withheld files.

The bottom line: Massie and Khanna's victory could renew one of the most disruptive Hill fights of the president's second term — but not until after the critical midterm election.

  • Khanna's post read, "We will not rest until the Epstein abusers are held accountable and there is justice."

item.title: Why Sydney Sweeney's nude ad struck such a nerve with women athletes
item.description:
A sports-betting ad featuring a semi-nude Sydney Sweeney triggered a backlash across women's sports, with female athletes flooding social media with a countermessage: This is what women in sports actually look like.

The big picture: Ads have long sexualized women, but the Novig ad's appeal to the male gaze hit differently at a moment when female athletes have cultural cachet and the platforms to push back.

Driving the news: Highlight reels of women diving, pitching, tackling, shredding, lifting, skating, sprinting, leaping and covering sports have flooded social media this week — all with the same core message.

  • British sprinter Amy Hunt delivered that refrain on-air this week, smiling and out of breath after the World Athletics Ultimate Championship: "Sydney Sweeney, this is what women in sport look like: 21.4. Muscles. Hard work, blood, sweat, tears," referring to American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden's winning time.

Women's sports are in an era of rapid momentum: The NCAA reported record high women's participation earlier this year, while Bank of America predicted U.S. women's sports revenue will grow more than 250% by 2030.

  • There's still a long way to go on screen time, says Purdue University professor Cheryl Cooky, who studies sports and gender. But she says traditional media increasingly covers women's sports more seriously.

Still, Cooky says, "it's in some ways not surprising that we get [the] Sydney Sweeney ad at this moment," describing it as "part of a backlash to the kinds of gains that women's sports, and by proxy, women more generally, are making in our society."

  • Some online argued the ad wasn't meant to portray a female athlete and was instead targeting sports bettors, who are more likely to be men.
  • But Cooky says it still struck a nerve because "we thought we were past the point of having to make a case that women in sport contexts are not simply sexual objects for male consumption."

Between the lines: Even if traditional media has made progress in covering women's athletics, corporate marketing tends to follow the cultural mood, explains Carly Drake, an expert on gender marketing at North Central College.

  • When feminism is prominent, brands sell empowerment. When the pendulum swings the other way, advertising can reinforce that backlash against women.
  • "It really legitimizes the viewpoint that women and other vulnerable groups don't belong in sports," she says.
  • Other sports- and fitness-related ads have recently faced criticism for their portrayal of women, including apparel brand Good Good for an ad where its co-founder shoved a female golfer to the ground.

Marketing in 2026 is a conversation, not a one-way channel, Drake explains, and social media offers a new generation of women in sports a way to build fan bases, shape their brands, and, in cases like these, resist.

  • "They're not being given this power. They're taking it," Cooky says. "They're creating their own narrative on social media, as opposed to 30 or 40 years ago, having to hope that … traditional media outlets and gatekeepers would call attention to these issues."

Zoom out: That's also spilled over into a boom of podcasts hosted by or about female athletes or women in the sports world, like hall-of-famer Sue Bird's "Bird's Eye View" and "We Can Do Hard Things" with soccer legend Abby Wambach,

  • Meanwhile, Apple TV hit "Ted Lasso" has returned to fictional team AFC Richmond. But no, not the guys from last season — now, it's the Lady Greyhounds on the pitch.

The bottom line: The male gaze isn't new. Women athletes' power — and access to platforms — to answer to it is.

item.title: Warren Buffett steps down as Berkshire Hathaway chairman
item.description:
Warren Buffett will step down as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, less than a year after handing over the CEO reins, the company said Friday.

The big picture: The "Oracle of Omaha" is 96, and his insurance-to-railroads conglomerate is moving onto a new generation, with his son Howard as chairman.

  • "Father Time always wins," Buffett said in a letter to shareholders announcing the news.

What they're saying: Buffett said the time was right to step aside from leading the board, after transitioning the CEO role to Greg Abel earlier this year.

  • "Greg runs the company; Howard will guard its culture and values – both worth more than anything on our balance sheet," Buffett wrote.
  • "Think of Howard as a policy the shareholders own and hope never to claim against."

Zoom in: Berkshire said Warren Buffett would become "chairman emeritus" and remain on the board of directors.

  • Long-time board member Susan Decker, the former president of Yahoo, will remain lead independent director.

By the numbers: Berkshire shares were flat in pre-market trading on the news.

  • The stock has underperformed this year, rising just 1% versus a gain of about 12% for the S&P 500.
  • If that doesn't change, it'd mark the fifth time in the last 10 years that Berkshire underperformed that benchmark.
  • While Berkshire has beaten the S&P by nearly 10 percentage points since 1965, in the last decade it's lagged the index by half a point or so.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with new details throughout.

item.title: Oil's shrug emoji era
item.description:
And the award for honesty in oil market analysis goes to ... J.P. Morgan!

  • "For the first time since the start of the Iran conflict, we don't have a baseline view. We simply don't know how to model the endgame," bank researchers said in a note (emphasis added).

Why it matters: While the phrasing is unusually blunt, the sentiment is shared to varying degrees.

  • Market watchers have come to grips with the likelihood that the status of the Strait of Hormuz — and the number of barrels getting through — will be messy for months to come.

The big picture: At the outset of the Iran war, J.P. Morgan's "Oil Markets Weekly" crew assumed there were "economic red lines" the White House would not cross.

  • The list includes $100 oil; gasoline near $5 per gallon; and 10-year Treasury yields hitting 5% (higher levels raise borrowing costs).
  • And still: "Six months later, many of those lines have been crossed, yet the exit strategy is less clear, not more."

The intrigue: The ongoing disruption of Middle East barrels, even if Hormuz transit has risen in recent weeks, will keep eroding the market's shock absorbers.

  • That said, lower oil demand has done more work than expected to ease stress on supplies, which has enabled a slower drawdown of countries' oil stockpiles, the J.P. Morgan note argues.
  • So "fears of inventories being close to exhausted as a balancing mechanism are premature," and there's an ample cushion to keep prices relatively contained "for now."

Yes, but: Even if crude prices haven't soared as high as many predicted when the strait was first choked off, soaring energy costs and shortages are creating pain, anger and unrest in many nations worldwide, the New York Times reports.

What we're watching: Uncertainty is also affecting dealmaking.

  • Elevated yet volatile prices are shaking up mergers and acquisitions in the exploration and production sector, per the consultancy Rystad Energy.
  • The conflict has "acted as both a headwind and a tailwind," a new note states. High prices are leading more companies — including U.S. shale producers — to test the market.

State of play: The value of opportunities in the global M&A market has swelled to $137 billion, yet volatile prices are "widening valuation expectations" and making transactions harder to pull off.

  • Rystad expects more flexible deal structures and stronger safeguards if transactions fall apart "as buyers and sellers seek to share commodity-price and closing risk."

The bottom line: "Oil price volatility has created a deeper opportunity set, but it has also made deals harder to execute," Rystad's Atul Raina writes.

item.title: "The Axios Show": Hasan Piker wants to campaign for AOC in 2028
item.description:
Left-wing streamer Hasan Piker said he "absolutely" wants to campaign for New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez if she runs for president in 2028 and said he has talked with AOC and her team, he said in the new episode of "The Axios Show."

Why it matters: Piker, who has millions of followers online, has been a high-profile campaign surrogate this year for a new generation of left-wing candidates, and wants to do the same in 2028.

Driving the news: Despite Piker's ambitions, some Democratic politicians have begun distancing themselves from him because of his controversial commentary.

  • Abdul El-Sayed, Michigan's Democratic nominee for the Senate, campaigned with Piker during the Senate primary.
  • But after Piker told Axios that he believed America's long history of attacks in the Middle East that have killed civilians made it worse than al-Qaeda "pound for pound," El-Sayed said he disagreed and that Piker didn't speak for his campaign.
  • El-Sayed has said Piker won't appear with him in the final weeks of the race before the Nov. 3 election.

In an hour-long interview with Axios, Piker explained his worldview and defended his stances that some Democrats are distancing themselves from:

China: Piker traveled to China last year and has said that the country is the closest government model he would like to see adopted in the U.S.

  • He also thinks that "trajectory-wise, I worry that a Chinese child might have better conditions in the next decade or next two decades than an American one. And I think that should worry every American citizen."

Asked about his past praise of Mao Zedong, Piker said "he's a great man of history. Of course, there were a lot of excesses."

  • When asked to clarify what he meant as "excesses," Piker said: "Deaths born out of mismanagement and famine."

Political violence: Axios asked Piker about several of his past statements about killing or harming political opponents, and he said they amounted to "three or four choice quotes."

  • He said he consistently says that the "appropriate way to deal with political problems, even violent ones, is to advocate, organize, and create a response that is born out of labor militancy, work stoppages and the like, to apply political pressure that way."
  • Talking with a friend on his stream, Piker once said of landlords who don't rent their properties: "Kill those motherf*ckers and murder those motherf*ckers in the streets. Let the streets soak in their f*cking red capitalist blood, dude."
  • He told Axios that "we were messing around. It wasn't a serious call to violence."

Piker — a frequent and aggressive critic of Israel's government — said he believes "Zionism is fascism" and that it was equivalent to neo-Nazism.

  • Asked about the potential danger of his rhetoric, Piker said: "I'm not worried that [my followers are] going to be violent against Zionists. No, I'm not."

item.title: Inside the scramble for trusted AI cops
item.description:
A host of industry players, policy wonks and businesses are grappling with the question of how to regulate AI in a trustworthy manner.

  • Inside the White House, it's mostly business as usual.

Why it matters: The industry's mad dash is the product of an ad hoc regulatory apparatus and a general consensus that swift action from Washington is unlikely in the near term.

State of play: AI CEOs have been grappling with how to test advanced AI and work with Beijing on safety standards, while the White House favors a solution where the industry finds ways to police itself.

  • That means the race is on to decide who will be anointed as third-party evaluators of AI systems and controls as the companies await legislation or White House action beyond the current voluntary process.
  • A robust ecosystem of safety and benchmarking groups already exists, but some White House officials and AI execs see them as too closely tied to top AI companies. Other options include businesses and startups that already do evaluations, as well as some more unorthodox suggestions.

What they're saying: Companies have the most expertise when it comes to AI and understand what the White House's AI voluntary framework requires, according to a White House official.

  • "These people are not 12-year-olds," the official said.
  • "The top frontier companies need to come to a consensus on what they want because they haven't agreed on anything," the official continued. "If these companies feel it's such a dire situation, they have every right, reason and ability to throttle their models."

Friction point: Some third-party evaluators — including individuals at METR, which investigated the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident — have been singled out for having close ties to the effective altruism movement, as well as to companies they would be policing.

  • One of the lead outside investigators of the Hugging Face episode is married to Paul Christiano, a seasoned AI safety and technology official who recently joined the board of OpenAI's nonprofit foundation. An Anthropic employee recently left the startup to work at METR as well.
  • METR has said it doesn't take funding from frontier labs. A spokesperson said Christiano joined the OpenAI board after the investigation concluded.
  • AI companies and safety officials say the AI research community has always been small and close-knit, and employees from frontier labs are well-suited to evaluate model capabilities.

Between the lines: Some facets of existing AI evaluation systems grew out of efforts to market the capabilities of new models, including how they perform on coding benchmarks and math tests.

  • A wide array of companies, including defense and tech contractor Booz Allen, evaluate AI systems for clients.
  • Many evaluations lack critical components, such as gauging how often models create software vulnerabilities or the variability in how they respond to prompts, said Eric Syphard, Booz Allen's head of AI.
  • "They all lean into that performance-only view of the world," Syphard told Axios in an interview.

Elon Musk this week suggested labs in the U.S. and China could review each other's models, a prospect some see as unlikely due to the ferocious competition between top players.

  • Other ideas have surfaced as well, including one former Trump adviser's call for legendary "coding god" and programmer John Carmack to step in.

OpenAI offered a public incident reporting playbook this week after identifying six new incidents.

  • Like the White House's AI framework, OpenAI's idea for public incident reporting is voluntary, as is Musk's peer review approach.
  • OpenAI's public incident reporting idea involves third-party auditors for more complex cases.

Yes, but: "Public transparency is really important here. What these companies are doing is good, but it's only based on their goodwill and I don't think that's sufficient," SaferAI executive director Henry Papadatos said in an interview.

What we're watching: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who will lead talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend, said there's an opening for safety talks with Beijing.
item.content:encoded:
A host of industry players, policy wonks and businesses are grappling with the question of how to regulate AI in a trustworthy manner.

  • Inside the White House, it's mostly business as usual.

Why it matters: The industry's mad dash is the product of an ad hoc regulatory apparatus and a general consensus that swift action from Washington is unlikely in the near term.

State of play: AI CEOs have been grappling with how to test advanced AI and work with Beijing on safety standards, while the White House favors a solution where the industry finds ways to police itself.

  • That means the race is on to decide who will be anointed as third-party evaluators of AI systems and controls as the companies await legislation or White House action beyond the current voluntary process.
  • A robust ecosystem of safety and benchmarking groups already exists, but some White House officials and AI execs see them as too closely tied to top AI companies. Other options include businesses and startups that already do evaluations, as well as some more unorthodox suggestions.

What they're saying: Companies have the most expertise when it comes to AI and understand what the White House's AI voluntary framework requires, according to a White House official.

  • "These people are not 12-year-olds," the official said.
  • "The top frontier companies need to come to a consensus on what they want because they haven't agreed on anything," the official continued. "If these companies feel it's such a dire situation, they have every right, reason and ability to throttle their models."

Friction point: Some third-party evaluators — including individuals at METR, which investigated the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident — have been singled out for having close ties to the effective altruism movement, as well as to companies they would be policing.

  • One of the lead outside investigators of the Hugging Face episode is married to Paul Christiano, a seasoned AI safety and technology official who recently joined the board of OpenAI's nonprofit foundation. An Anthropic employee recently left the startup to work at METR as well.
  • METR has said it doesn't take funding from frontier labs. A spokesperson said Christiano joined the OpenAI board after the investigation concluded.
  • AI companies and safety officials say the AI research community has always been small and close-knit, and employees from frontier labs are well-suited to evaluate model capabilities.

Between the lines: Some facets of existing AI evaluation systems grew out of efforts to market the capabilities of new models, including how they perform on coding benchmarks and math tests.

  • A wide array of companies, including defense and tech contractor Booz Allen, evaluate AI systems for clients.
  • Many evaluations lack critical components, such as gauging how often models create software vulnerabilities or the variability in how they respond to prompts, said Eric Syphard, Booz Allen's head of AI.
  • "They all lean into that performance-only view of the world," Syphard told Axios in an interview.

Elon Musk this week suggested labs in the U.S. and China could review each other's models, a prospect some see as unlikely due to the ferocious competition between top players.

  • Other ideas have surfaced as well, including one former Trump adviser's call for legendary "coding god" and programmer John Carmack to step in.

OpenAI offered a public incident reporting playbook this week after identifying six new incidents.

  • Like the White House's AI framework, OpenAI's idea for public incident reporting is voluntary, as is Musk's peer review approach.
  • OpenAI's public incident reporting idea involves third-party auditors for more complex cases.

Yes, but: "Public transparency is really important here. What these companies are doing is good, but it's only based on their goodwill and I don't think that's sufficient," SaferAI executive director Henry Papadatos said in an interview.

What we're watching: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who will lead talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng this weekend, said there's an opening for safety talks with Beijing.

item.title: Blanche warned of contempt risk in Epstein files case
item.description:
A federal judge warned Attorney General Todd Blanche Wednesday that he could face contempt proceedings if the Department of Justice fails to comply with an order involving the release or review of Epstein files.

Why it matters: The case could force the DOJ to release additional Epstein records or remove redactions that a court determines aren't permitted under the law.

What they're saying: U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan wrote in a 20-page order Wednesday that a civil contempt charge would be "premature" for now, but warned it could become appropriate if Blanche fails to comply with the court's renewed order.

  • "[C]ourts have the inherent power to enforce compliance with their lawful orders through civil contempt," Sullivan wrote.
  • "A contempt finding is proper where 'the putative contemnor has violated an order that is clear and unambiguous' and the violation of an order is 'proved by clear and convincing evidence.'"

The other side: "Our filings will speak for themselves," a DOJ spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement.

  • "We have already shown the Judge proof of redacted victim names and established that the plaintiff in this case seeks to unmask victim names."

Catch up quick: Independent journalist Katie Phang brought the lawsuit, alleging the DOJ hasn't released all documents required under the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which Congress passed last November.

  • Sullivan said last month he didn't want to start contempt proceedings, but added that the public "has a right to know what the hell is going on in this case" and the "victims have a right to know and the court has a right to know."

Zoom in: Sullivan ruled Wednesday that the DOJ provided adequate documentation showing some email redactions were made to protect survivors' privacy.

  • But he said the department hadn't provided enough documentation to justify redactions in other emails and ordered it to provide additional documentation for private "in camera review" — a process in which a judge reviews confidential, sensitive or privileged documents outside public view.
  • The judge rejected the DOJ's assertion that handwritten FBI notes were "properly withheld because they are 'substantially similar to' and therefore duplicative of the typewritten reports." He said the DOJ's review protocol does not require withholding "substantially similar" records.
  • Sullivan also rejected the DOJ's argument for not reviewing foreign-language materials related to Epstein because it was "not practicable for a first-level reviewer to determine the responsiveness of a foreign-language document."

Yes, but: Sullivan acknowledged that some redactions covered the names and email addresses of a government attorney and law enforcement personnel, which the DOJ's review protocol requires to be redacted.

State of play: The lawsuit is one of several seeking additional transparency or alleging DOJ errors related to the Epstein files, which have generated legal and political scrutiny of the Trump administration.

  • Congress has held U.S. attorneys general in contempt before, including Eric Holder during the Obama administration and William Barr during Trump's first administration.
  • The DOJ did not respond to Axios' request for comment.

What we're watching: A House discharge petition is two signatures shy of forcing a vote on the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, which would enforce and expand the release of remaining DOJ files.

  • Outgoing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is leading the effort, as he did with Act I.

Go deeper: House GOP's Epstein files headache is back

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a DOJ statement.

item.title: Exclusive: Scalise puts GOP high-water mark at 225 House seats
item.description:
House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) is staring at a scary political environment for Republicans and claiming to see something very different: a path to 225 seats.

Why it matters: Republican leaders insist they can retain the majority, but only if they drive their voters to the polls by manufacturing the kind of voter enthusiasm Democrats are generating organically.

  • "If we make it a contrast election, we win," Scalise told Axios in an interview Thursday.
  • "We could get to 225. It would be a good night for us if we did, but it's possible," he said.
  • "235 is not," he said. "You're literally doing coin tosses in a couple of seats."

Between the lines: Asked if he saw any signs of a blue wave forming or the map expanding, Scalise said: "Not right now. No."

Reality check: Republicans know that history — and many of the indicators heading into November — is working against them.

  • "I know what history says, you know, but history's not on the ballot," Scalise said.
  • Still, Democrats are turning out in primaries — and special elections — as if they're getting free gas cards for showing up.

Democrats lead by nearly nine percentage points on the generic ballot.

  • President Trump's approval rating is below 40%, according to the RealClearPolitics average.
  • And Trump is underwater by a whopping 61 percentage points on inflation in a recent poll, an apparent record.

Zoom in: Republicans are examining the map with a jeweler's loupe and insist the picture isn't as bleak in the pivotal battleground seats.

  • "We're not looking at national polls; we go district by district," Scalise said.
  • That means trench warfare in 35 seats, where Republicans say they have proven winners, plenty of money and new rules to spend it.
  • "We've got 20 [seats] on our side that we're fighting to hold on to that are real competitive, and 15 [seats] that we have a real chance to flip," he said. "These are knock-down, drag-out fights."

What we're hearing: The White House has long thought of the midterms as a "hate election." Scalise uses the more genteel term "contrast election."

  • But before Republicans can dream about growing their majority, they need to fix their enthusiasm problem — and match the Democratic energy showing up in many of the preelection indicators.

The GOP's midterm convention in Dallas last week was the first step.

  • "If we are able to capitalize on that kind of enthusiasm and carry that momentum into November, then we'll have the same turnout as the other side, and we'll hold the majority," Scalise said.
  • Now comes the road show: Congressional leaders — and the president — are hitting the campaign trail.
  • In the next two weeks, Scalise will travel to 11 states to campaign for 16 Republicans — incumbents and challengers.

The bottom line: The 225-seat scenario is Scalise's high-water mark. At another point in the interview, he suggested the majority could be smaller — closer to the 220–215 split Republicans won in 2024.

  • "This isn't going to be a 10-seat majority, but it could be a six-seat majority."

item.title: Scoop: Trump expected to meet with Venezuela's new leader
item.description:
President Trump is making plans for a first-ever meeting with Venezuela's interim president, Delcy Rodriguez, as early as next week, sources familiar with the discussions tell Axios.

Why it matters: The potential meeting showcases the close relations between the nations under Trump. But it's also fraught with political risks that extend from Miami to Caracas.

Driving the news: Trump is already planning to meet with Gulf leaders at the UN General Assembly in New York next week to discuss the Iran War, and those who know his thinking say he wants to make time for a sidelines sit-down with Rodriguez as early as Tuesday, sources said.

  • "Iran is tough, but Venezuela is without a doubt the president's top success and Delcy is a key to that," a Trump adviser said. "Unless something goes really wrong, the president wants to make time."
  • A senior administration official cautioned: "Nothing is finalized. This is up to the president."
  • On Sunday, when asked about meeting Rodriguez, Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One that "I may be, I may be."

Zoom in: The New York City meeting could happen just blocks from the federal lockup where Rodriguez's predecessor and onetime ally, socialist Nicolas Maduro, awaits trial on narco-terrorism charges.

  • Maduro was seized Jan. 3 in Caracas in a U.S. military operation authorized by Trump.
  • Rodriguez assumed power after the coup and has worked closely with Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to normalize relations between the countries, including the inking of a massive but controversial Venezuelan oil deal first reported by Axios.

Friction point: Clustered in South Florida, conservative and vocal Venezuelan exile community has expressed increasing agitation with the administration for working so closely with Rodriguez, a lifelong socialist who rose to power along with Maduro under strongman Hugo Chavez, both foes of the U.S. this century.

  • Adding to the anger in the diaspora: neither Trump nor Rubio has called for elections in Venezuela, despite years of bashing Maduro as an election-stealing dictator.
  • Supporters of Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Corina Machado also grew frustrated with administration officials over their criticism of the exiled Venezuelan political leader when she tried to return home after the earthquakes in June.

The big picture: In Florida, politicians, pollsters and consultants say higher gas prices due to the Iran war and the administration's heavy-handed immigration enforcement are bigger political problems for Republicans in the midterm elections than promoting democracy now in Venezuela.

  • Polls in Venezuela show Rodriguez and Trump have low favorability ratings and Machado has the highest, although it's declining.
  • Some in Trump's orbit have expressed concern that the optics of a meeting with Trump will hurt Rodriguez even more at home because she could look like too much of a U.S. puppet.
  • But Trump isn't concerned about that, the administration official said, noting "The fact is POTUS loves Delcy because she's delivering and she's leading."

item.title: Inside House Democrats' behind-the-scenes food fight
item.description:
The House's last in-session week before the midterms was beset by furious private finger-pointing between House Democrats following several high-profile rebellions.

Why it matters: This dynamic may only worsen if Democrats retake the House, which is set to see an influx of distinctly rebellious and independent lawmakers, particularly on the left.

  • There is even chatter among members contrasting the ability of House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to control members with that of his top deputy, Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.), according to two House Democrats.
  • Said one of the lawmakers, speaking on the condition of anonymity to share details of sensitive private discussions: "People are talking about 'mom and dad'. … Dad is soft."
  • "I think people are asking the question: If this is happening in the minority, are you prepared for what will happen in the majority?" said a third House Democrat.

"There is no daylight between the three of us," Jeffries said at a Thursday press conference with Clark and Democratic Caucus chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.).

  • "We'll address the situation when we address the situation," he added.
  • A Democratic leadership aide told Axios that everything Jeffries' deputies do is in coordination with him and doesn't represent a break between leaders.

Driving the news: Reps. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez (D-Wash.) and Jared Golden (D-Maine) on Tuesday provided Republican leadership with the necessary votes to advance a package of GOP bills, including a Russia sanctions bill strongly opposed by Democratic leaders.

  • It was the second time this month the pair of centrists defected from leadership on a procedural vote — even after Clark and Jeffries publicly threatened them with punishment the first time.
  • "People thought the first time was a mistake. The second time is defiance," said a fourth House Democrat, telling Axios the two "operate like they are above the caucus."
  • Clark, along with Jeffries, engaged Gluesenkamp Perez in a heated discussion on the House floor during the vote in view of an Axios reporter, which sources said was about her defection.

The rebellion came after Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) forced a vote on impeaching President Trump without support from leadership.

  • The vote angered many House Democrats, who complained Green was muddying the party's message on a crucial week.
  • Jeffries and Clark voted "present" along with 44 other Democrats. 147 sided with Green and 18 voted with Republicans to quash the impeachment effort.
  • Leadership's neutrality on that vote drew frustration as well, with a fifth House Democrat telling Axios: "Our constituents don't send us here to be 'present.' They send us here to use our judgment."

What they're saying: OurRevolution executive director Joseph Geevarghese said Jeffries "never seems to have this much trouble figuring out what to do when progressives are in his sights."

  • "You cannot demand discipline from progressives while treating defections to the right as an unsolvable procedural dilemma," he told Axios.
  • Rep. Analilia Mejia (D-N.J.) said progressives "catch shit" for being "too ideologic and bold on our ideas," and that it's "curious ... how there isn't an equally vocal attack" on centrists who break from the party line.
  • Usamah Andrabi, a spokesperson for the left-wing Justice Democrats: "Leadership is threatening a Democratic majority in November by refusing to stand up to the corporate Democrats aiding and abetting Republicans' agenda."

What we're hearing: Jeffries isn't the only target of rank-and-file backlash — Clark is getting heat from moderates for taking a swipe at Gluesenkamp Perez.

  • The minority whip told reporters Wednesday that "it's team players who should sit on exclusive committees," which was widely interpreted as a reference to Gluesenkamp Perez's seat on the Appropriations Committee.
  • Fumed a sixth House Democrat: "Katherine Clark just declared on moderate Democrats, which is a risky move for leadership going into a potentially tight majority."
  • Jeffries' has been far more muted, repeatedly saying he will "have more to say about the situation when I have more to say about the situation."

Much of the fury is also directed at Golden and Gluesenkamp Perez, with some of it is coming from their fellow centrists.

  • "Everyone in the caucus is sick of the bullshit. Everyone has their ... number," a seventh House Democrat, a moderate, told Axios.
  • "Marie is playing with fire," a senior House Democrat told Axios, adding that Jeffries "may not do anything now, but her committee appointment may be in jeopardy for next session."

The other side: Gluesenkamp Perez said in a statement to Axios, "I don't worry about that kind of stuff. I will always vote my District and let others play inside DC politics games."

  • Said Golden: "I'm a Mainer and an American. I'm also a proud Democrat, but that team is a distant third."

The bottom line: "Members have concerns about those who are not team players," a ninth House Democrat told Axios, and "next year is the best time to address it."

  • Golden, who is retiring, has a warning for his colleagues: "Be careful what you wish for. Next time, it could be you facing punishment for putting your constituency or our country ahead of the party."

The bottom line: "Members have concerns about those who are not team players," a ninth House Democrat told Axios, and "next year is the best time to address it."

  • Golden, who is retiring, has a warning for his colleagues: "Be careful what you wish for. Next time, it could be you facing punishment for putting your constituency or our country ahead of the party."
